a233.speaker: Atupele Muluzi, United Democratic Front (UDF) leader
a233.speech: Has raised alarm over what he describes as a growing threat to democracy, warning that Malawi is on a dangerous path toward autocratic rule and internal decay; speaking at the Platform for African Democrats conference last month, he said that Malawi is experiencing a rollback of democratic principles amid rising global instability and weakening international cooperation. "We are witnessing a dangerous shift: a retreat from the principles that have long underpinned democratic governance," Atupele said. "Truth itself has become a casualty, with disinformation distorting the foundations of informed political discourse."

a233.speaker: Atupele Muluzi, United Democratic Front (UDF) leader
a233.speech: Pointed to the consolidation of power by autocratic regimes across the continent, adding that such trends have emboldened leaders who undermine democracy through coercion rather than consent ; linked these regional developments to Malawi, accusing the current administration of using undemocratic tactics to cling to power; did not provide specific details on the alleged tactics, but urged Malawians to resist any attempts to subvert democratic norms.

a233.speaker: Atupele Muluzi, United Democratic Front (UDF) leader
a233.speech: Highlighted the impact of shrinking international support, citing the scaling back of donor agencies such as USAid, the US Agency for International Support; warned that Africa is being left to tackle economic stagnation, agricultural insecurity, corruption and poor governance largely on its own.

a233.speaker: Atupele Muluzi, United Democratic Front (UDF) leader
a233.speech: Further accused several African governments of falling prey to kleptocracy, describing them as "government by the corrupt, for the corrupt," where leaders prioritise personal enrichment over public service.

a233.speaker: Atupele Muluzi, United Democratic Front (UDF) leader
a233.speech: Alleges that government officials threatened him with arrest following his critical remarks during a radio interview; Muluzi declared, "Our democracy must be defended, and I will not back down. If speaking the truth is a crime, then bring it on!" ; contends that the government employs intimidation tactics to silence opposition political parties and dissenting voices, thereby undermining democratic principles.

a233.speaker: Atupele Muluzi, United Democratic Front (UDF) leader
a233.speech: Has spoken against government's handling of the economy, pointing to issues such as rising unemployment and inflation; has also accused the administration of persistent corruption and failing to address public concerns effectively, contrary to President Lazarus Chakwera's promises to end graft ; according to Atupele, lower-level officials often feel pressured to tolerate corrupt behaviour from their superiors, further entrenching the problem.

a233.speaker: Atupele Muluzi, United Democratic Front (UDF) leader
a233.speech: Has declared his intention to run in Malawi's 2025 presidential election, indicating that talks for a potential electoral alliance conceived to unseat Chakwera are underway. In a recent statement, he affirmed: "I will be on the ballot, and Malawians will vote for me as President." ; He stresses: "Above all, Malawi should have food." ; "I am my own man," said Atupele, declaring his commitment to progressive politics aimed at finding solutions to the nation's pressing challenges.

a233.speaker: Ezekiel Ching'oma, Minister of Homeland Security of Malawi
a233.speech: In response, challenged him to provide evidence of the alleged threats, questioning the legitimacy of his claims.

a233.speaker: Transparency International (report)
a233.speech: According to Transparency International, corruption remains a pervasive issue, affecting all levels of government.

a233.speaker: Activists
a233.speech: Described the amended colonial prison law / correctional facilities as focusing more on punishing inmates than reforming them.

a233.speaker: Afrobarometer opinion polls (surveys)
a233.speech: Surveys, including Afrobarometer opinion polls, indicate that a majority of Malawians prefer democratic governance to authoritarian alternatives.

a271.speaker: Keir Starmer, UK Prime Minister
a271.speech: countered and derided Badenoch for attempting to mislead the public over claims that her push for increased defence spending necessitated cuts to the UK's foreign aid budget. He dismissed her claim as a "desperate search for relevance", while in the same breadth mocking her as one who appointed herself as "the saviour of western civilisation."

a271.speaker: Kemi Badenoch, leader of the Conservative Party and the Opposition in the UK
a271.speech: In a speech delivered to a conservative audience not long ago, Badenoch painted a bleak picture of Nigeria, describing it as a country plagued by corruption and inefficiency.

a376.speaker: Joe Biden, President of the United States
a376.speech: Welcomed on Thursday the death of Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, speaking of a “good day for Israel, the United States and the world,” which removes a major “obstacle” to a ceasefire in the Gaza Strip and the release of the hostages ; “It is now possible to envisage a 'day after' in Gaza without Hamas in power, as well as a political settlement offering a better future for Israelis and Palestinians alike” (statement) ; “Yahya Sinwar was an insurmountable obstacle to achieving all of those objectives. That obstacle no longer exists” ; “I called (Bibi) Netanyahu to congratulate him on eliminating Sinwar. He had a lot of blood on his hands.” “It is now time to move forward.” ; Announced that he was dispatching Antony Blinken to Israel in “four or five days”; recalled in his statement that after the Hamas attack he had ordered US intelligence services to help their Israeli counterparts to “locate and track Sinwar and other Hamas leaders.”

a376.speaker: Kamala Harris, US Vice-President and candidate for the White House
a376.speech: Said that this gave “the opportunity to finally end the war in Gaza” ; “This war must end in such a way that Israel is secure, the hostages are released, the suffering in Gaza ends and the Palestinian people can exercise their right to dignity, security, freedom and self-determination,” she told the press from Milwaukee.

a376.speaker: Israel (government announcement)
a376.speech: Announced on Thursday that Yahya Sinwar, considered the architect of the October 7, 2023 attack against Israel, had been killed during an operation on Wednesday in the Gaza Strip.

a376.speaker: Office of the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu
a376.speech: According to the Israeli Prime Minister's office, the two leaders considered that the death of Mr Sinwar constituted “an opportunity to facilitate the release of the hostages” and that they would “cooperate in order to achieve that objective.”

a376.speaker: Jake Sullivan, US National Security Adviser
a376.speech: Insisted that the United States was not involved in the operation: “This was an operation of the Israeli army,” he told journalists accompanying the American president ; Speaking of an “incredibly significant blow” dealt to Hamas, emphasised the opening that presents itself to try to revive ceasefire negotiations, which have been at a standstill since the summer, while saying it was “too early” to know the impact on the Palestinian Islamist movement.

a376.speaker: Antony Blinken, US Secretary of State
a376.speech: Said he wanted to “redouble efforts with our partners in the region” in order to create “a new path” towards peace.

a376.speaker: Matthew Miller, US State Department spokesman
a376.speech: Said that Blinken had already spoken on Thursday with his Qatari and Saudi counterparts.

a376.speaker: United States (government)
a376.speech: On Tuesday threatened Israel with suspending part of its military assistance if there was no significant improvement in humanitarian aid in the besieged Gaza Strip, giving it a 30-day deadline.

a779.speaker: Residents of Keetmanshoop (spoken to by nbc News)
a779.speech: Said they started queuing as early as six o'clock in the morning at the Ministry of Gender Equality, Poverty Eradication, and Social Welfare's Conditional Basic Income Grant registration.

a779.speaker: Mommies, a grassroots group at Okahandja
a779.speech: Is calling for urgent intervention from the Ministry of Gender Equality, Poverty Eradication, and Child Welfare over the increasing number of underprivileged children in the town.

a779.speaker: George Simataa, Secretary to Cabinet
a779.speech: Has announced the appointment of three new Executive Directors in the public service.

a779.speaker: Marginalised communities living in Bwabwata National Park
a779.speech: Say they are finding it difficult to bury their dead, largely due to bureaucratic processes.

a899.speaker: Johnson Motshwarakgole, union leader (Botswana Manual Workers Union)
a899.speech: Urged members to ignore toxic gossip lampooning him and other union leaders as sellouts for not supporting the ‘Ntlole’ proposal for the rest of the public servants, adding that although it would have benefited the already highly paid workers at other cooperating unions, supporting such would have spelt doom for the lowly paid workforce.

a899.speaker: Johnson Motshwarakgole, union leader
a899.speech: Said he was recently booed at a teachers union conference and called all sorts of names as they accused him of selling the manual workers to the ruling Botswana Democratic Party (BDP) during the negotiations.

a1187.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a1187.speech: Has commended the Government of Malawi for holding productive and constructive discussions with the new administration during the Fund's annual meetings held earlier this month in Washington, D.C.

a1187.speaker: Julie Kozack, IMF spokesperson
a1187.speech: Said the institution was encouraged by the engagement and looks forward to supporting Malawi's efforts to stabilize its economy and implement meaningful reforms. "We look forward to continuing discussions on the authorities' plans to restore macroeconomic stability and on how the IMF can best support their reform efforts."

a1187.speaker: Joseph Mwanamveka, Minister of Finance and Economic Development of Malawi
a1187.speech: Recently emphasized that an IMF-supported programme is vital for unlocking donor confidence and strengthening partnerships with international financial institutions. "An IMF programme is key to rebuilding trust with our development partners and opening doors to much-needed financial support."

a1201.speaker: Lester Kapanda, researcher at Kamuzu College of Health Sciences
a1201.speech: said vaccines for rotavirus have made a difference. "Malawi, rotavirus used to kill more than 2,500 young children per year, and just two years after Malawi introduced the rotavirus vaccine, hospital admissions for the disease fell by 43 per cent," Kapanda said.

a1201.speaker: Maziko Matemba, health rights activist
a1201.speech: said the 2024-25 national budget has already indicated a declining commitment to the health sector. Compared to last year, where 12.2 percent of the national budget was allocated to health, this year's allocation has dropped to just 9.5 percent. "The reduction comes at a time when demand for healthcare services continues to rise, making the shortfall even more alarming," Matemba said.

a1201.speaker: Mathews Ngwale, Chairperson for the Parliamentary Health Committee
a1201.speech: acknowledged the severity of the situation, saying that global health financing is largely shaped by major donors like the US government. "The US plays a crucial role in driving health investments, not just through government agencies like USAID but also through private foundations and individual donors," he said.

a1201.speaker: Sam Mndolo, Principal Secretary in the Ministry of Health
a1201.speech: said the issue is not much about filling the gap but rather ensuring that the essential services that were previously supported by the resources that have been withdrawn continue. "This distinction is important because not all of the quoted amount—whatever the precise figure may be— was directly allocated to service delivery. Additionally, even for funds that were used for service delivery, it is crucial to assess whether they supported cost-effective interventions and whether they were utilised through cost-effective delivery channels," he said. To address this challenge, he said, the ministry has taken several strategic steps including re-prioritization of services, improving efficiency in resource utilisation and exploring financial health reforms.

a1201.speaker: Reports (cited source)
a1201.speech: USAID has been a dominant force in Malawi's health sector, injecting about $185 million annually to support various programmes, including HIV/Aids treatment, maternal health, and vaccination campaigns, according to reports.

a1227.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a1227.speech: said on Wednesday that governments in sub-Saharan Africa have provided school meals to roughly 20 million extra children over the past two years, showing a move away from dependence on foreign aid and a stronger commitment to education.

a1227.speaker: WFP report
a1227.speech: said “Government investments in school meals … (signal) a significant shift from reliance on foreign aid to recognising school meals as a strategic public investment in children’s education (and) health.”

a1227.speaker: U.N. report (end of July)
a1227.speech: found that more than one in five Africans, 307 million, were chronically malnourished, meaning hunger is worse than two decades ago, and predicted the continent would have 60% of the world’s hungry people by 2030.

a1227.speaker: WFP report
a1227.speech: found that local farmers had also benefited from the school feeding: the government of Benin’s buying local food for these programmes contributed over $23 million to the economy in 2024, and more than a third of school meals in Sierra Leone came from food produced by smallholder farmers.

a1227.speaker: WFP report
a1227.speech: warned, however, that millions of children, especially in some of the lowest income African countries like the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Somalia, and South Sudan, still lacked access to school meals, as donor support continued to fall.

a1230.speaker: Non-Governmental Organisations Regulatory Authority (Ngora)
a1230.speech: says forex tracking and coordination remains a challenge in the sector.

a1230.speaker: Innocentia Ottober, Ngora board chairperson
a1230.speech: made the remarks on Friday during the 2025 NGO Day commemorations at Mzuzu Stadium; said there have been some improvements in monitoring due to the Exchange Control Regulations; explained that Ngora is also finalising a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM) to improve monitoring ; “We recognise the boost to domestic liquidity that will be brought by the recent Exchange Control Regulations requiring conversion of foreign currency into Malawi kwacha.”

a1230.speaker: Innocentia Ottober, Ngora board chairperson
a1230.speech: said in 2025 the NGO sector reported a total income of K1.017 trillion, with K747 billion received in foreign currency, mainly US dollars, British pounds and euros ; “These inflows make a significant contribution to Malawi’s foreign exchange reserves, supporting humanitarian interventions and the wider economy.”

a1230.speaker: Innocentia Ottober, Ngora board chairperson
a1230.speech: on funding challenges facing the sector due to aid cuts by major development partners such as the United States Agency for International Development, called for “a deliberate shift towards domestic resource mobilization, stronger compliance, fairer distribution of resources across the sector and investment in local institutional capacity.”

a1230.speaker: Jean Sendeza, Minister of Gender, Community Development and Social Welfare
a1230.speech: delivering her keynote address, commended Ngora’s collaboration with RBM in improving forex tracking, saying that will ensure resources are used in line with national priorities ; “The recent Exchange Control Regulations will enhance domestic liquidity while supporting NGOs with foreign-denominated obligations.”

a1230.speaker: Jean Sendeza, Minister of Gender, Community Development and Social Welfare
a1230.speech: in response to concerns by some NGOs over the 80 percent mandatory conversion of forex, said the regulations were made in consultation with the NGOs: “All NGOs are aware that we need to have these regulations. And as a country, we just cannot be doing business as usual. We need to follow the legal framework.”

a1230.speaker: NGOs under the banner of National Advocacy Platform
a1230.speech: expressed fear last month that the 80 percent mandatory conversion could affect their operations.

a1230.speaker: Exchange Control (Management of Non-Governmental Organisations and Public Sector Foreign Currency Receipts) Regulations of 2025 (document)
a1230.speech: reads in part: “The Bank shall apply a mandatory conversion or retention ratio of 80 percent of the total funding credited in a holding foreign currency-denominated account, at the official buying exchange rate, published by the Bank. A holding foreign currency-denominated account holder that requests the transfer of funds in accordance with sub-regulation shall complete and submit a bank transfer instruction to its bank, and the bank shall immediately submit a request to the Bank for release of the funds to the operating account of the requesting institution. Where the funds requested will be used within Malaŵi, the Bank shall transfer the funds so requested to the authorised dealer bank in the Malaŵi currency equivalent, converted using the official buying exchange rate published by the Bank, on the day the transfer is effected.”

a1291.speaker: Stephen Mhando, Public Relations and Communications Manager at Geita Gold Mining Limited (GGML) and Kili Trust Fund Manager
a1291.speech: "This challenge is a physical test, promoting the proactive role we can all take in maintaining our own health and wellness and a dedication to sustaining progress in the national response to HIV & AIDS." ; "GGML is proud to walk this journey with our partners, contributing to community health and collective action."

a1291.speaker: Stephen Mhando, Public Relations and Communications Manager at GGML
a1291.speech: said the 2025 event will be held under the theme "What if we gave up?" highlighting the importance of persistence, partnership and continued investment in one of the continent's most persistent public health challenges.

a1424.speaker: Situmbeko Musokotwane, Zambian Finance Minister
a1424.speech: Presented the budget in Parliament with an allocation of N$40-million to each of the 156 constituencies to decentralise development, with 81% of the budget to be sourced locally.

a1615.speaker: A diplomat representing a Western nation (unnamed envoy to Tanzania)
a1615.speech: Said on September 19, 2024 that his country will not retreat from its push for strict adherence to democratic rights and principles as a key aspect for its partnership with Dodoma; according to his statement, his nation had the right and authority to intervene in Tanzania's internal political affairs because of the aid it provides.

a1615.speaker: Samia Suluhu Hassan, President of Tanzania
a1615.speech: Warned other countries to desist from interfering in Tanzania's internal affairs and violating the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations by trying to dictate how the government should handle its internal matters.

a1615.speaker: Embassy of the Western nation in Tanzania (statement, 1 October 2020)
a1615.speech: Issued a threatening statement and warned that if electoral procedures were not adhered to, they "will not hesitate to consider consequences for those found to be responsible for election-related violence or undermine the democratic process."

a1615.speaker: The same Western nation (statements at various times)
a1615.speech: Issued threatening statements, saying that the country "would watch closely the actions of individuals who interfere in the democratic process and will not hesitate to consider consequences including visa restrictions for those responsible for election-related violence."

a1615.speaker: Some Western countries
a1615.speech: Regard China's non-interference policy as indifferent to people's aspirations for democracy, civil liberty and defending of human rights, hence immoral and undesirable.

a1615.speaker: Chinese Foreign Ministry spokespersons
a1615.speech: Its position before, during and after the Tanzanian elections held on 28 October 2020 was that China believed the Tanzanian government and its people had the wisdom and capability to organise elections without any external interference, and called on all countries to respect the non-interference principle, support African countries' independence and safeguard their unity and stability.

a1854.speaker: International Food Policy Research Institute (Ifpri), analysis of the economic and welfare implications of the reduction of US foreign assistance in Malawi
a1854.speech: Says it expects the situation to result in gross domestic product (GDP) loss of $127 million (about K222 billion) this year, and projects that by 2030 the six-year cumulative GDP losses will likely amount to $1.3 billion (about K2.3 trillion) with over half-a-million additional people falling into poverty trap. Reads the analysis in part: "By 2030, Malawi's economy will be $304 million [about K532 billion] smaller than it would have been in the absence of the US foreign assistance shock. ; The combination of reduced employment opportunities and suppressed wages following the contraction of the service sector and higher costs of living driven by rising import prices affect welfare outcomes in Malawi." ; Ifpri said under the current exchange rate regime, the official rate of the kwacha does not respond to changes in dollar supply, which limits the economy's ability to self-correct, leading to persistent US dollar shortages. Based on a list of cancelled and retained awards and information on 2024/25 disbursements, Ifpri estimates that US foreign assistance to Malawi could decline by 59 percent in 2025.

a1854.speaker: US State Department
a1854.speech: According to the US State Department, USAid, the hitherto biggest development agency on the planet, was giving $350 million (about K630 billion) to Malawi annually.

a1854.speaker: Reserve Bank of Malawi (RBM)
a1854.speech: Said it is devising strategies to cushion the economy from the impact of the temporary ban on foreign aid imposed by the US.

a1854.speaker: Boston Maliketi Banda, Reserve Bank of Malawi spokesperson
a1854.speech: Is on record as having said the temporary ban on foreign aid is a concern for many developing countries, including Malawi: "This is one of the reasons the governor [of RBM] has embarked on an engagement drive with key stakeholders to collaboratively develop practical and implementable strategies to address such shocks and sustainably address the forex supply shortages in the country."

a1854.speaker: Greenson Nyirenda, Catholic University economics lecturer
a1854.speech: Said in an interview on Wednesday that the loss could worsen the country's foreign exchange crisis, which has dampened forex reserves to less than three months of import cover: "The funding by international organisations remains one of the significant sources of forex for countries such as Malawi that have low exportation capacity. This will hit them hard."

a1854.speaker: Velli Nyirongo, Scotland-based Malawian economist
a1854.speech: Warned that reduction in foreign exchange reserves could weaken the government's ability to meet external obligations and destabilise the exchange rate.

a1920.speaker: Players in the horticulture sector
a1920.speech: say the country needs to invest in technology for their products to meet global standards ; "I am convinced that Africa is a continent of opportunities. When it comes to fruit and vegetable agriculture,…"

a1920.speaker: Agriculture experts
a1920.speech: projecting the horticulture industry as the country's next big export earner.

a2081.speaker: Nigerian Tobacco Control Alliance (NTCA) and Corporate Accountability and Public Participation Africa (CAPPA) (joint press conference)
a2081.speech: Have urged the Federal Government to raise the allocation for the Tobacco Control Fund (TCF) from N13 million to at least N300 million in the 2025 national budget, citing the urgent need to address the public health crisis caused by tobacco use; acknowledged the increase from N10 million in 2024 to N13 million in 2025 but emphasised that this amount is inadequate to implement the National Tobacco Control Act 2015 effectively ; lamented that N13m remains grossly insufficient compared to the level of funding required; cited tobacco use as public health enemy number one responsible for millions of preventable deaths worldwide, including that of thousands of Nigerians yearly, and added that confronting this public health emergency requires financial commitment and full operationalisation of the TCF.

a2081.speaker: Akinbode Oluwafemi, CAPPA's Executive Director
a2081.speech: "We urge the government to prioritise the Tobacco Control Fund, increase the allocation to at least N300million as an urgent measure to stop the tobacco industry from causing more damage. The lives of Nigerians are at stake." ; "While the government drags its feet on adequate allocation to the Tobacco Control Fund, the tobacco industry is relentlessly lobbying the public to embrace newer, stylish kinds of harmful tobacco products and other so-called smokeless nicotine-filled products that it falsely presents as 'less harmful' or 'safer' than traditional tobacco use. These alternative nicotine products, including vapes, also known as electronic cigarettes (e-cigarettes) and other electronic nicotine delivery systems (ENDS), heated tobacco products (HTPs), snus, and oral nicotine pouches, among others, are targeted at our teeming, impressionable youth population which the industry sees as a potential replacement for the thousands of others who die or whose lives are destroyed by tobacco use."

a2081.speaker: Olawale Makanjuola, Alliance Coordinator of NTCA
a2081.speech: Called for transparency in administering the TCF, noting that increasing the sum in the budget, without efficient deployment of same to tobacco control efforts would be counterproductive; advised the government through the Ministry of Health and Social Welfare to comply with the law in administering the TCF: "The National Tobacco Control Act requires that funds allocated for tobacco control in the national budget or from other sources are to be remitted to the Tobacco Control Fund account for utilization. We urge the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare to provide regular updates on the status of the Fund, including its balance, sources of the monies in the Fund and details of expenditures."

a2081.speaker: Michael Olaniyan, Country Coordinator for the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids
a2081.speech: Warned of the dangers of Nigeria's failure to act on the TCF: "Every day Nigeria fails to adequately fund tobacco control, more lives are lost. Our youth are targeted by deadly marketing, and our health system edges closer to total collapse under the weight of preventable diseases. The cost of inaction is measured in cancer wards filled with the young and a future mortgaged to addiction and death. If the government does not act now with a substantial budgetary allocation to the Tobacco Control Fund, they are not just failing in local and global commitment to health policies - we are failing our people. The time to seriously fund TC is now."

a2081.speaker: CAPPA and NTCA (joint statement)
a2081.speech: The statement noted that effective sensitisation campaigns need robust media outreach, deep community engagement, and active coordination with various stakeholders across the country, all of which require substantial funding: "Furthermore, enforcement and monitoring activities are crucial to combat industry interference and ensure compliance with tobacco control regulations. This includes prosecuting violations, safeguarding smoke-free spaces and ensuring a ban on tobacco advertising, promotion and sponsorship, amongst other efforts." ; noted that despite longstanding stakeholder calls, the TCF has yet to be fully operationalised, allowing tobacco companies to exploit Nigeria's weak monitoring systems.

a2081.speaker: CAPPA and NTCA (joint statement)
a2081.speech: "Right now, Nigeria's tobacco control efforts depend on donor funding, which is not inexhaustible. Many countries were caught flatfooted by the Trump Administration's scraping of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID). Nigeria must not wait until that happens before it takes action to protect the health of its people against the onslaught of the tobacco industry. It must adequately increase the tobacco control fund."

a2205.speaker: BBC
a2205.speech: Reported confirming a leaked memo's contents, that the US State Department has issued a halt to nearly all existing foreign assistance and paused new aid, according to an internal memo sent to officials and US embassies abroad.

a2205.speaker: US State Department internal memo (leaked notice)
a2205.speech: The notice appears to affect everything from development assistance to military aid, making exceptions only for emergency food aid and for military funding for Israel and Egypt. It adds that US officials "shall immediately issue stop-work orders, consistent with the terms of the relevant award, until such time as the secretary shall determine, following a review." It also orders a wide scale review of all foreign assistance to be completed within 85 days to ensure the aid adheres to President Trump's foreign policy goals. The memo also said waivers have so far been approved by Rubio for "foreign military financing for Israel and Egypt and administrative expenses, including salaries, necessary to administer foreign military financing."

a2205.speaker: US government figures
a2205.speech: The United States is the world's biggest international aid donor spending $68bn in 2023 according to government figures.

a2205.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a2205.speech: Has previously stated that all US spending abroad should take place only if it makes America "stronger", "safer" or "more prosperous" ; Rubio's memo, justifying the freeze, said it was impossible for the new administration to assess whether existing foreign aid commitments "are not duplicated, are effective and are consistent with President Trump's foreign policy" ; has issued a waiver for emergency food assistance, according to the memo.

a2205.speaker: Josh Paul, former senior State Department official who oversaw Congressional relations on weapons transfers until late 2023
a2205.speech: Told the BBC the notice meant a "potentially huge" impact on foreign aid programs funded by the US. "One can imagine, for example, the humanitarian de-mining programs around the world suddenly being told stop work. That's a pretty big deal."

a2205.speaker: Dave Harden, former USAID mission director in the Middle East
a2205.speech: Told the BBC the move was "very significant", saying it could see humanitarian and development programs funded by the US around the world being immediately suspended while the review is carried out, and that it could affect a wide range of critical development projects including water, sanitation and shelter. "The employees of the implementing partner or the [non-governmental organisation] would be able to be paid, but actual assistance, I think, needs to be halted." ; "I have gone through [assistance suspensions] many times when I was the West Bank and Gaza mission director, but that was specific to that account. This is global." ; "Not only does it pause assistance, but it puts a 'stop work' order in existing contracts that are already funded and underway. It's extremely broad."

a2205.speaker: AFP news agency
a2205.speech: Reported the funding freeze could also potentially affect Ukraine, which received billions of dollars in weapons under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.

a2205.speaker: US State Department
a2205.speech: The State Department has been approached for comment (no response given).

a2485.speaker: Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, President of Ghana
a2485.speech: Said the coming on stream of the power project represented a landmark initiative and a transformative step forward in the country's pursuit of energy security, economic growth and sustainable development ; said the project, which started in April 2017, represented a vision grounded in the country's desire to harness cutting-edge technology and innovative solutions to power the future ; said the new plant had not only fulfilled expectations but was also an example of the nation's strength, resilience and unity in achieving shared goals ; said that reliable power supply was not only convenient but was the foundation of modern progress and national development: "It is the force that drives factories, powers hospitals, illuminates classrooms and provides opportunity and dignity for every citizen" ; said the project would provide essential power to the national grid to reduce pressure on existing infrastructure: "We can now look forward to greater power stability, and bring relief to households and businesses alike. This is a meaningful step forward toward our national energy goals and delivering of consistent quality power to every corner of the country."

a2485.speaker: Herbert Krapa, Minister of State at the Ministry of Energy of Ghana
a2485.speech: Commended President Akufo-Addo for leading what he termed "a remarkable accomplishment and a contribution of 200MW to the generation capacity at a time when demand is increasing ever so rapidly" ; "Our commitment as a government to ensure reliable and affordable supply of electricity for domestic and industrial use remains non-negotiable, and this addition from bridge power goes a long way to consolidate energy security while fostering economic growth."

a2485.speaker: Reginald France, General Manager of Early Power Ltd
a2485.speech: Described the plant as a groundbreaking facility, and an ultra-modern infrastructure powered by advanced technology from GE: "This underscores our dedication to providing reliable, efficient and sustainable energy solutions to the people of Ghana."

a2485.speaker: Reginald France, General Manager of Early Power Ltd
a2485.speech: "We plead with the government to eagerly honour its obligations to Early Power and other independent power producers in the country. We believe that access to reliable electricity is a fundamental right and catalyst for economic growth and social progress."

a2485.speaker: Brain Herlihy, Chief Executive of Endeavour Energy
a2485.speech: Said the project would have a significant impact on life, adding that reliable electricity was fundamental to advancing industry, improving health care, supporting education and lifting communities.

a2485.speaker: Virginia Palmer, US Ambassador to Ghana
a2485.speech: Also said that the project was "a testament to what could be achieved when we come together with a shared vision and commitment as we look to the future."

a2485.speaker: David Boadi Asamoah, acting Managing Director of ECG
a2485.speech: Said the project represented a major step forward, reinforcing the collective goal of achieving energy security and ensuring that every citizen had access to reliable electricity.

a2577.speaker: Senior official from the Ministry of Homeland Security (anonymous)
a2577.speech: disclosed that the discussions follow announcements by UNHCR and WFP that they can no longer fund support for refugees in Malawi: "With UNHCR and WFP pulling out, we are left with no option. Malawi cannot continue shouldering the burden of hosting refugees without international support."

a2577.speaker: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and World Food Programme (WFP)
a2577.speech: announced that they can no longer fund support for refugees in Malawi.

a2577.speaker: Innocent Magambi, Inua Advocacy Chief Executive Officer
a2577.speech: praised Malawi's history of hospitality but warned against forced or coerced returns: "Malawi has shown immense generosity by hosting refugees despite economic hardship. However, forced repatriation to volatile regions such as eastern DRC or politically sensitive countries is not only unlawful but dangerous." ; He urged the government and its international partners to consider alternative, rights-based solutions such as local integration, lifting the encampment policy and targeted support for vulnerable groups: "By enabling refugees to become self-reliant, Malawi could reduce its long-term financial burden and preserve its international human rights standing."

a2577.speaker: Charles Kajoloweka, Youth and Society Executive Director
a2577.speech: cautioned the government against a blanket repatriation policy, warning that returning refugees to unsafe environments would violate human rights: "We understand the government's constraints, but the solution is not to force people back into danger. Stakeholder dialogue is essential to finding a balanced, humane approach."

a2577.speaker: Steven Kayuni, Secretary for Homeland Security
a2577.speech: said he was attending a meeting and did not respond to our questionnaire.

a2588.speaker: United Nations
a2588.speech: according to which no less than 20.9 million Ethiopians need emergency humanitarian assistance, which requires 1.7 billion dollars to pay for.

a2588.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a2588.speech: tweeted over a short video showcasing Sheger Park, inaugurated on September 10, 2020, with public officials' social media feeds emphasising unity, forgiveness and togetherness, and quotes declaring the country will yet prosper and "ascend to prestige."

a2588.speaker: Amnesty International
a2588.speech: according to which law enforcement used lethal force, unnecessarily, in the Welaita Zone, where the demand for regional status by citizens claimed the lives of over 15 people.

a2588.speaker: House of Federation of Ethiopia
a2588.speech: declared the elections that took place in the Tigray Regional State "unconstitutional" in their undertaking and said the outcome is "illegitimate."

a2588.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a2588.speech: made repeated commitment - in public - that force will not be resorted to in dealing with the refractory Tigray Regional State; he and officials of the ruling Prosperity Party (PP) strongly opposed the Tigray regional elections.

a2588.speaker: Ethiopian Citizens for Social Justice (Ezema)
a2588.speech: has been unhappy with the state of affairs in the capital; it accused those in charge of the Addis Abeba City Administration of land grabs and breaking public trust, transferring condominium units initially built for those who were registered and had saved their money.

a2588.speaker: National Movement of Amhara (NAMA)
a2588.speech: demanded transparency and accountability in the expenditure and contract administrations of the many projects ongoing in the capital.

a2588.speaker: European Union
a2588.speech: called last week for a political settlement through an all-inclusive and comprehensive dialogue.

a2685.speaker: Government of Tanzania
a2685.speech: Has challenged the universities to speed up commercialisation of academic research, focusing on the industry, transport and banking sectors, to support the country’s development. The government said by fostering closer collaboration between the universities and these industries, can help address real-world challenges, create jobs and contribute significantly to the development agenda.

a2685.speaker: Prof Kitila Mkumbo, Minister of State in the President’s Office for Planning and Investment
a2685.speech: Said it’s important to speed up the collaboration between universities and the private sector in advancing practical, solution-oriented research. “Let us invest in innovation and research instead of prioritising sports sponsorship,” the minister said when officiating University of Dar es Salaam (UDSM) 10th Research and Innovation Week on Monday.

a2685.speaker: Prof Kitila Mkumbo, Minister of State in the President’s Office for Planning and Investment (on foreign aid and research funding)
a2685.speech: Noted that relying solely on foreign aid for research is no longer sustainable, urging instead for stronger partnerships with local private institutions to fund innovation to strengthen the nation’s economy ; Proposed the establishment of a National Startup Fund and called on the private sector to actively collaborate universities to mobilise research funding and support commercialisation efforts.

a2685.speaker: Prof Lilian Kaale, UDSM Head of Department of Food Science and Technology, College of Agricultural Science and Food Technology (CoAF)
a2685.speech: Painted the need to align academic research with national priorities. “Researches should not remain on papers rather disseminated to the public, government and the private sector for meaningful application,” she said. She also acknowledged a common challenge, while many projects successfully reach the prototype stage, most fail to scale due to a lack of thorough evaluation ; “Studies show that many projects that successfully complete the Research and Development prototype phase still fail to reach large-scale deployment…ended up in ‘technology Death Valley’.”

a2685.speaker: Prof Nelson Boniface, UDSM Deputy Vice-Chancellor - Research
a2685.speech: Said that building a sustainable digital infrastructure is essential for innovation, calling for investments in reliable and scalable systems. He said that through Research and Innovation Week nine private sector partners with UDSM focused on digital technology to promote local solutions and support startup growth.

a2695.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a2695.speech: Said today in the city of Quelimane, Zambezia province, that the violent post-election protests caused damage calculated at 1.5 billion meticais: "We have taken note and we are going to visit some districts, because of the violent, criminal and illegal demonstrations. Zambezia province suffered great losses; these losses are calculated at 1.5 billion meticais - that is a great loss." ; "That is why, I repeat, we cannot destroy our own house again, because tomorrow we may need these things that we are destroying. It happened that people destroyed fuel pumps and the next day they woke up and found that they have money but nowhere to fill up the vehicle, because they destroyed the fuel pump." ; Noted that there were cases of individuals who went out to burn certain infrastructure and the next day intended to promote further demonstrations because of the shortage of food and fuel and the rise in prices resulting from the violent, criminal and illegal demonstrations.

a2695.speaker: Government of Mozambique
a2695.speech: Guarantees that it is working to carry forward the structuring projects, namely the Mocuba bridge and the roads linking the districts of Zambezia, among others that were foreseen under the financing of the North American government, the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA).

a2695.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a2695.speech: "We are taking the decision that next year, rain or shine, cold or not, with or without the MCA, we are going to build the bridge and the roads."

a2695.speaker: Government of Mozambique
a2695.speech: On the port of Macuzi, in Zambezia province, affirms it is working with all stakeholders in order to get the project started.

a2695.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a2695.speech: "We came to realise that there are many interests. What we did was to bring these brothers of ours together and we are on a good path, all the parties are reconciling. As we are holding talks, at any moment we will resume the resettlement that was already being carried out in Macuzi. The port of Macuzi will develop Zambezia, it will bring a lot of employment for our youth."

a2695.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a2695.speech: On Zambezia's agricultural potential and the port of Quelimane: "Zambezia is a province rich in agriculture; it is no accident that it was the place where the prazeiros lived, the fundamental basis being agriculture. These lowlands of ours produce rice, maize, all kinds of beans, what the world needs."

a2695.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a2695.speech: Reported that Zambezia province is rich in mineral and tourism resources, which is why on this working visit he will travel to the district of Pebane and others: "We are going to Pebane, we are going to other districts where investment had already been attracted, where people had already started working and receiving a salary, for example in the heavy sands extraction project; we want to work so that this project does not stop."

a2695.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a2695.speech: Stressed that the government is aware that, because of various cyclones such as Dikeledi, Chido and others that affected Zambezia province, several roads linking administrative posts, localities and districts are degraded: "We are going to work to repair our roads and we will continue working so that agriculture, tourism, everything that is potential, can happen. We are going to build the Mocuba bridge, the roads of Zambezia, roads, the Port of Macuzi, the headquarters of the Assembly of the Republic, the parliamentary citadel, and we are going to develop Zambezia."

a2695.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a2695.speech: On peace and security: "For there to be peace, there must be harmony, reconciliation, no hatred. Let us all, as Mozambicans, fight hate speech and violence; let us promote peace, forgiveness and development."

a2695.speaker: Daniel Chapo, President of the Republic of Mozambique
a2695.speech: Added that the government is committed to development, which is why it approved the Local Economic Development Fund, whose launch is scheduled for next week, in order to stimulate economic development and support people in need, to foster businesses and projects generating employment and income.

a2745.speaker: Dismissed Project Hope Namibia-Malawi staff member (anonymous)
a2745.speech: “They said there was no money to pay us—but somehow, they're still drawing massive salaries while we can't even buy food for our families,” one dismissed staff member told Nyasa Times.

a2745.speaker: Former Project Hope Namibia-Malawi employee (anonymous)
a2745.speech: “Where is the justice?” cried one former employee. “We were tossed out like garbage, left to starve, while top executives keep cashing in. Is this what USAID stands for?”

a2745.speaker: Former PHN-MW employees (collectively)
a2745.speech: Called what happened “blatant discrimination, abuse of power, and financial injustice” and are demanding justice; called for urgent intervention from USAID and the US Embassy, Malawi Labour Authorities and independent auditors, demanding immediate payment of all outstanding salaries and benefits, reinstatement of contracts now that the project is back, and a full investigation into PHN-MW's financial management and ethical conduct; ex-staff say PHN-MW hasn't remitted pension contributions since December 2024.

a2745.speaker: Project Hope Namibia-Malawi (PHN-MW) management
a2745.speech: Cited lack of funds in terminating over 3,000 employees, and told former employees they must reapply for their jobs; promised to pay workers up to March 10th.

a2745.speaker: United States Government (“stop work” order)
a2745.speech: In January 2025 issued a “stop work” order temporarily pausing project activities pending a review; the order did not authorize contract terminations. On March 24, 2025, the USG lifted the suspension and authorized all implementing partners to resume work.

a2745.speaker: Dr. Endale, PHN-MW Chief of Party (non-response)
a2745.speech: Attempts to reach him were unsuccessful; he did not respond to calls or messages, fueling further frustration among former employees.

a2863.speaker: Beninese government
a2863.speech: Accuses Patrice Talon, promoter of the company Benin Control, of seeking to destabilise the institutions of the Republic, presenting him as a stateless man who has made an attempt on the life of the institutions of the Republic

a2863.speaker: Eugene Dossoumou, Secretary General of the Government of Benin (formal notice letter No. 233/PR/SGG/SGAG3/C)
a2863.speech: “In the hope that you will comply with this formal notice, the government assures you that it is in the name of democracy that it wishes to send it to you in a spirit of adversarial debate, because increasingly you appear as a citizen determined to defy and humiliate a government and to make the suicidal choice of destabilising the institutions of the Republic.” ; “This is an inadvisable option to which an absolute end must be put because it carries the seed of endangering the peace, stability and security that have always characterised our dear homeland.”

a2864.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
a2864.speech: Committed to advancing Liberia's interests on the global stage through targeted collaborations and proactive representation, emphasised the transformative potential of strong bilateral relations with France and its European partners and highlighted the need to prioritise development goals, particularly in education, infrastructure, and trade. “Our partnership with France is an untapped reservoir of opportunities. As ambassador, my goal will be to translate these opportunities into tangible benefits for our country.”

a2864.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
a2864.speech: Underscored economic diplomacy as the cornerstone of his strategy, describing it as a tool to attract foreign direct investments (FDIs) and boost local industries, and cited France's role as a major global economy and its potential as a key partner for Liberia in trade, agriculture, and industrial development. “I intend to position Liberia as an attractive destination for French investors. By engaging key stakeholders in France's private sector, we can open new markets for Liberian products, especially in agriculture, which remains the backbone of our economy.” ; Said he is cognizant of the importance of improved relations with France, which was the second European nation after the United Kingdom to have officially recognized Liberia's sovereignty in 1852, and that he is aware France is part of the Group of Seven (G7) informal bloc of industrialized democracies

a2864.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
a2864.speech: Pointed to the importance of ensuring that economic gains benefit ordinary Liberians. “It's not just about bringing investments, but ensuring that those investments create jobs, improve livelihoods, and contribute to national development.”

a2864.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
a2864.speech: Spoke extensively about leveraging Liberia's membership in global bodies such as UNESCO and vowed to enhance Liberia's participation in education, culture, and scientific initiatives promoted by UNESCO, noting that these programs align with Liberia's national priorities; said he will ensure the Permanent Delegation of Liberia to UNESCO remains a consequential member of the organization. “UNESCO offers immense opportunities in education and cultural preservation. As a nation rich in culture and history, we must make our voice heard and access the support needed to improve our education system and preserve our heritage.”

a2864.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
a2864.speech: Acknowledged the existing cooperation between Liberia and France in various sectors, including the training of security forces and French language promotion, and pledged to strengthen these collaborations, particularly in addressing pressing challenges like climate change and sustainable development

a2864.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
a2864.speech: Highlighted his commitment to inclusive development, with a particular focus on youth empowerment and gender equity, and stressed the importance of giving young Liberians access to education, training, and opportunities abroad. “Investing in our youth is investing in our future. Through scholarships and exchange programs, we can equip the next generation of Liberians with the skills needed to drive our country forward.” ; “Gender equality is not just a moral imperative; it is a developmental necessity. Women must be given equal opportunities to contribute to Liberia's growth.”

a2864.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
a2864.speech: Committed to advocating for increased international support to address environmental challenges and noted that France, as a leader in global climate initiatives, can play a significant role in supporting Liberia's environmental sustainability efforts. “Climate change is a shared challenge that requires shared solutions. We will work closely with France to secure resources and expertise to protect our forests, preserve biodiversity, and promote renewable energy.”

a2864.speaker: Dr. Teeko T. Yorlay, Sr., Liberia's Ambassador Designate to France
a2864.speech: Highlighted his readiness to bring his extensive experience in governance and policy implementation to bear in his new role. “I am fully prepared to serve Liberia with diligence and integrity. If confirmed, I will dedicate myself to achieving measurable results for the Liberian people.” ; Expressed gratitude for the trust placed in him by President Joseph N. Boakai and reiterated his commitment to putting Liberia's interests above all else: “This nomination is not just an honor; it is a call to serve. I am committed to working tirelessly to ensure that Liberia's voice is heard, our partnerships are strengthened, and our people reap the benefits of these efforts.” ; “Our success will not be measured by words but by actions and outcomes. Together, we can build a Liberia that is respected internationally and thriving domestically.”

a2864.speaker: Members of the Senate Committee on Foreign Affairs
a2864.speech: Commended Dr. Yorlay for his clear vision and readiness to serve as Liberia's top diplomat in France

a2864.speaker: Senator Abraham Darius Dillon, Chair of the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee
a2864.speech: Described Yorlay as “a nominee with a wealth of experience and a strong sense of patriotism.”

a2992.speaker: Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA)
a2992.speech: Has announced a waiver of penalties for vehicles in use and present in the country but which have various tax problems; the waiver, which began on August 01 and ends on December 31, 2025, will cover vehicles brought in under temporary importation that have remained in the country, vehicles that entered Tanzania Mainland from Zanzibar without following customs procedures, transit vehicles retained in the country, vehicles granted tax exemption whose ownership was transferred to persons not entitled to the exemption, and transit vehicles whose permitted period expired without an extension.

a2992.speaker: Yusuph Mwenda, TRA Commissioner General (statement)
a2992.speech: In a statement issued by the TRA Commissioner General, Yusuph Mwenda, the Authority explained that it has been facing challenges in managing these vehicles on which duty and taxes were not paid at the time of importation, and so TRA has officially announced an amnesty period from August 01, 2025 to December 31, 2025, during which the owners of the vehicles concerned will be required to come forward to pay duty and taxes while all interest and penalties are waived. ; "In accordance with section 70(1) of the Tax Administration Act, Chapter 438, and Section 249 of the East African Community Customs Management Act of 2004, the Commissioner General of the Authority grants a tax waiver to owners of the types of vehicles mentioned… which were brought into the country knowingly or unknowingly without the relevant duty and taxes having been paid." ; "During the amnesty period, the owners of the vehicles concerned will be responsible for paying the relevant amount of duty and taxes; the interest and penalties will all be waived."

a2992.speaker: Tanzania Revenue Authority (TRA)
a2992.speech: TRA stated that vehicles in the listed categories that are seized after 31 December 2025, and on which duty and taxes have not been fully paid, will be dealt with in accordance with the law, including criminal prosecution, with those involved required to pay the duty and taxes, together with penalties and interest.

a3124.speaker: Government of Owambo
a3124.speech: Is surprised that the four churches made the statement on the reasons for the emigration of Ovambos available to the press; it was under the impression that the memorandum continued to serve as a basis for discussion and would not be published unilaterally, and for this reason has so far refrained from issuing a statement of its own.

a3124.speaker: Government of Owambo
a3124.speech: Has issued no statement on yesterday's talks. (non-response)

a3124.speaker: Church leaders of ELOK, the Roman Catholic Church, the Anglican Church and the Baptist congregation (joint memorandum)
a3124.speech: Presented the Commissioner-General with a memorandum on the reasons why the Ovambos are leaving their country; they thank the Commissioner-General for having invited them “in these difficult times” to talks with the leaders of the government on the question of why people are leaving the country, and ask him to see to it that the talks of 27 June and 6 August “may bring not mistrust, hatred, persecution and misunderstanding, but good fruits of peace.”

a3124.speaker: African Party for the Independence of Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde (PAIGC)
a3124.speech: Wishes for a link between Bissau and the Cape Verde Islands.

a3124.speaker: Richard Nixon, President of the United States
a3124.speech: Has declared anew that he will not resign, although strong pressure is now being exerted on him to avoid a conviction by the Senate.

a3124.speaker: Senator Barry Goldwater
a3124.speech: Even Senator Goldwater, who is highly regarded by Nixon, has now come out in favour of Nixon's resignation; as a member of the Senate's political committee, which sent a delegation to the White House to tell the President that he was in danger of being convicted if he did not resign beforehand.

a3124.speaker: South African Council of Churches (SACC) resolution
a3124.speech: In the resolution the member churches are called upon to urge all their members to consider “whether the call of Christ to take up the cross and follow him, and in doing so to identify with the oppressed, does not in our situation mean the refusal (of military service) on grounds of conscience”.

a3124.speaker: Major-General J. A., Chaplain-General of the South African armed forces (statement)
a3124.speech: Said in a statement that the English-speaking clergy had taken note with dismay of the Council of Churches' resolution encouraging South Africans to refuse military service; the chaplains, familiar with the aims and methods of the communist-inspired terrorists “who want to penetrate our country through murder and violence”, call on all church members, and especially young men, to make their personal contribution to the defence of the country; the chaplains remained loyal to South Africa and expressed their thanks to the army for the opportunity to realize their calling as proclaimers of the Gospel.

a3177.speaker: Hassan Kiazulu, Former Montserrado County Representative (serving as proxy for Finance Minister Augustine Ngafuan)
a3177.speech: Says resource mobilization is a skill that requires narrowing the fiscal space of Liberia, leading the transformation of Monrovia ; Wants authorities at the Monrovia City Corporation (MCC) to complement national allocations with strategic local revenue generation to realize such a transformation ; Is encouraging government ministries and agencies to coordinate with the MCC as a means of redirecting the many challenges in Monrovia and its residents.

a3177.speaker: Alaric Tokpa, Acting Chairman of the Governance Commission
a3177.speech: Has stressed the need to rebuild Monrovia that is inclusive, resilient, and responsive for lasting development ; Wants Monrovia to be repositioned in the decentralized government system to put it on par with other modern cities around the world ; Indicated that the two-day dialogue is a deliberate and strategic intervention to generate the decision to reform the City of Monrovia.

a3177.speaker: John Siafa, Monrovia City Mayor
a3177.speech: "Unclear boundary disputes over service and administrative authority are a huge challenge that weakens planning and wastes the resources of Monrovia City Government" ; Disclosed that weak institutions and policy fragmentations are some of the challenges associated with service and waste deliveries for the MCC.

a3212.speaker: Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) (statement sent to the newsroom)
a3212.speech: According to a statement sent to our newsroom, the signing of the Financing Agreement between the Governments of Mozambique and the United States, through the MCC, is scheduled for September of this year, in Washington DC ; Compact II will focus on Zambézia province, covering three areas: Promotion of Investment in Commercial Agriculture; Rural Connectivity and Transport; and Climate Change and Coastal Development.

a3264.speaker: US government data
a3264.speech: According to US government data, total trade in goods between the United States and Africa was estimated at US$71.6 billion (€61.9 billion) in 2024.

a3264.speaker: Analysts
a3264.speech: Have warned that these US cuts in development aid could bring southern African countries, including Angola and Mozambique, closer to China.

a3264.speaker: US State Department (memo released to the press)
a3264.speech: A State Department memo released this week by the press shows that the travel-ban list may include 36 more countries -- 25 of them African, including Angola, Cabo Verde and Sao Tome and Principe; the memorandum identified several criteria which, in the US government's assessment, were not being met by these states, such as not having "any competent or cooperative central government authority to produce reliable identity documents or other civil documents" or suffering from "widespread government fraud".

a3264.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, President of the African Development Bank (AfDB)
a3264.speech: Warned of the economic consequences of the tariffs imposed by the United States on Africa, saying last month that 47 of the 54 African countries will be directly affected by this new US trade policy, which will potentially reduce these nations' export revenues and foreign exchange reserves ; Pointed out that although Africa accounts for about 20% of the world's population and less than 3% of global GDP, there is a scenario for growth: ten of the world's 20 most dynamic economies are in Africa.

a3364.speaker: Dr Vincent Zoma, Joseph Ki-Zerbo University (study, "Burkina Faso: mobility and terrorism, a crucial issue for development")
a3364.speech: Argues that mobility is essential to sustainable development but that in Burkina Faso the growing insecurity caused by terrorism compromises it, seriously affecting trade and increasing the vulnerability of populations, with transport infrastructure often targeted and certain regions rendered almost inaccessible; states that many once-safe roads have become impassable, that women and children are especially affected, and that farmers struggle to reach their fields or transport their produce, causing income losses and heightening food insecurity.

a3364.speaker: Dr Vincent Zoma, Joseph Ki-Zerbo University (study, "Burkina Faso: mobility and terrorism, a crucial issue for development")
a3364.speech: Proposes levers to restore mobility: that public policies integrate security, economic development and mobility, with investment in transport infrastructure, checkpoints and regular patrols, community involvement in surveillance, and promotion of alternative modes such as community transport; notes that community transport projects based on motorcycles or tricycles and "security corridors" have emerged; holds that international organisations play an essential role by financing infrastructure projects, modernising roads and training local actors, and that regional cooperation is paramount; and stresses that citizens' engagement — local committees, awareness-raising, youth transport cooperatives — is crucial. Concludes that the government must intensify efforts to restore security while collaborating with international partners, and that with strengthened local capacities, investment in infrastructure and reformed public policies, Burkina Faso can restore mobility and foster sustainable development.

a3364.speaker: United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), 2022 report
a3364.speech: According to UNHCR (2022), more than 2 million people are internally displaced, representing about 10% of the population.

a3364.speaker: Siry A. & Traoré I. (2023), "Effects of Insecurity on Inflation in Burkina Faso"
a3364.speech: Cited as the source for the finding that farmers struggle to access their fields or transport their produce, resulting in income losses and heightened food insecurity.

a3365.speaker: Ugandan social media users (#1986Pictures posts)
a3365.speech: Have been using social media to draw attention to President Museveni's unrestricted rule, and have, since January, used the hashtag #1986Pictures to tweet pictures showing how much had changed since he first came to power; many tweets were personal, speaking of how the users weren't even born in 1986, others highlighted the development of technology saying "in 1986 apples and blackberries were just fruits" or listed photos of Museveni with four successive American presidents.

a3365.speaker: Yoweri Museveni, President of Uganda
a3365.speech: On the day of the election, announced that Facebook, Twitter and WhatsApp had been blocked, as a security measure; he described social media as a "pathway of lies."

a3365.speaker: MTN (telecommunications company, tweet)
a3365.speech: Issued a tweet saying the Uganda Communications Commission (UCC) had directed them to disable all social media and mobile money services "due to a threat to Public Order and Safety."

a3365.speaker: Indian Supreme Court (1978 judgment)
a3365.speech: "If democracy means government of the people by the people, it is obvious that every citizen must be entitled to participate in the democratic process and in order to enable him to intelligently exercise his right of making a choice, free and general discussion of public matters is absolutely essential."

a3365.speaker: Legal Brains Trust (Ugandan NGO, court filing)
a3365.speech: Challenged the shutdown in court, seeking a declaration that the blocking by the UCC was unjustifiable and unlawful, and a declaration that the Attorney-General and the Bank of Uganda acted unjustifiably and unlawfully by not acting to restore access to the blocked sites; they also sought an injunction preventing the UCC from repeating the blockage, and an order instructing the Attorney-General to inform the court what measures he was undertaking to curb impunity in the communications sector.

a3365.speaker: European Union and Commonwealth election observers
a3365.speech: Have also criticised the handling of Thursday's poll (per the Reuters photo caption); opponents rejected the outcome of the election.

a3506.speaker: Jessie Kabwila, Minister of Higher Education of Malawi
a3506.speech: Says her ministry is seeking alternative funding to support at least 500 students in institutions of higher learning impacted by the withdrawal of United States (US)-funded projects. ; Said the ministry has been advising institutions of higher learning to use their own budgets to absorb students who were on USAid sponsorship: “But where institutions have exhausted all channels, the ministry has been engaging local and international partners to support the students.”

a3506.speaker: Malawi College of Health Sciences (MCHS)
a3506.speech: Appealed for assistance after losing K4.1 billion meant for student sponsorship, wages for specialised staff, learning materials and technology support following the withdrawal of USAid.

a3506.speaker: Steven John, 24-year-old clinical medicine student
a3506.speech: Said USAid was supporting him with K125 000 accommodation, K200 000 upkeep and K400 000 tuition per semester.

a3506.speaker: Alice Kadango, MCHS executive director (analysis made available to The Nation)
a3506.speech: Said the college has also lost support for 10 clinical instructors and six specialised lecturers for its degree programmes.

a3571.speaker: Council of Ministers of Benin (weekly cabinet meeting decision, 11 May 2016)
a3571.speech: Authorised the sale on national territory of timber, firewood and charcoal, until new directives are put in place in the sector; also decided to suspend the movement permits required for transporting forest products intended exclusively for national consumption, and provisionally authorised skidding and clearing operations for felled timber intended exclusively for national consumption.

a3571.speaker: Minister of Living Environment and Sustainable Development of Benin (communication to the Council of Ministers)
a3571.speech: Made the communication on the basis of which the Council of Ministers authorised the resumption of domestic trade in timber, firewood and charcoal.

a3571.speaker: Minister of State of Benin
a3571.speech: According to the Minister of State, the government remained firm on the ban on the export of forest products and instructed the Minister of the Interior, the minister in charge of transport and the minister in charge of living environment to ensure strict compliance with this firm prohibition; however, containers of processed timber already stored at the port of Cotonou before the precautionary measure was taken could exceptionally be exported, only after a joint inspection by the three ministries.

a3611.speaker: Thomas Nyarko Ampem, Deputy Finance Minister of Ghana
a3611.speech: Told a high-level panel at the 78th World Health Assembly in Geneva that Ghana is ramping up domestic resource mobilisation and exploring innovative health financing models to shield its health system from external aid volatility, and said the government is redirecting resources, deepening partnerships with the private sector, and introducing structural fiscal reforms to fund health services as donor funding continues to decline: “External aid is no longer a reliable solution. We must prioritise prevention, repurpose budgets, and unlock new investment through good governance and innovation.”

a3611.speaker: Thomas Nyarko Ampem, Deputy Finance Minister of Ghana
a3611.speech: Emphasised the need to reorient policy around primary health care and preventive services, saying the expanded access to clean water, sanitation, nutritious food and immunisation provided since January 2025 are foundational measures more cost-effective than treating diseases.

a3611.speaker: Thomas Nyarko Ampem, Deputy Finance Minister of Ghana
a3611.speech: On mitigating the abrupt withdrawal of US$78 million in USAID health support through the partnership with drone logistics firm Zipline: “Being responsive to change is critical. We leveraged technology and logistics to close urgent supply gaps and maintain continuity of care.”

a3611.speaker: Thomas Nyarko Ampem, Deputy Finance Minister of Ghana
a3611.speech: Cautioned that attracting private investment depends on improving governance and macroeconomic stability: “Without fiscal discipline, we cannot build the systems that attract long-term investment.”

a3611.speaker: Thomas Nyarko Ampem, Deputy Finance Minister of Ghana
a3611.speech: Said now is the time for the continent to translate its vision of health self-reliance into durable outcomes: “We must move with urgency, unity and foresight. This is our opportunity to build resilient health systems for the future.”

a3611.speaker: World Bank (estimates)
a3611.speech: Estimates that Africa’s health spending per capita remains significantly lower than in other regions, averaging just US$47 compared to more than US$4,000 in high-income countries.

a3611.speaker: 2024 Mo Ibrahim Index (report)
a3611.speech: According to the index, nearly half of Africa’s population now lives in countries where governance has worsened over the past decade.

a3776.speaker: Lydia Shilongo (22), DREAMS beneficiary and kiosk owner, Tsumeb, Namibia
a3776.speech: “My dream is to own 10 restaurants all over Namibia one day, and to employ many other vulnerable young women,” she envisioned.

a3776.speaker: Lydia Shilongo (22), DREAMS beneficiary and kiosk owner, Tsumeb, Namibia
a3776.speech: “I learnt about the programme from a DREAMS nurse while receiving HIV testing services and soon joined a Safe Space group with 16 other adolescent girls and young women, who call their group ‘Queen Empowered’,” shared Shilongo.

a3813.speaker: Dambisa Moyo, Zambian economist (in Dead Aid, 2009)
a3813.speech: argued that foreign aid has done more harm than good for Africa.

a3813.speaker: Akinwumi Adesina, former president of the African Development Bank

a3827.speaker: João Lourenço, Angolan President
a3827.speech: In his inaugural address to the US-Africa Summit in Luanda, launched a clear appeal to move from a traditional aid model to a dynamic of strengthened private investment, inviting American companies to see Africa no longer as a receptacle for humanitarian aid but as a land of economic opportunity with strong growth potential: « It is time to substitute the logic of aid with that of ambition and investment. Africa must be perceived as a credible partner, eager for capital, skills and win-win cooperation » ; insisted on the continent’s transformation, stressing that Africa is no longer a passive beneficiary but a dynamic zone, conducive to innovation, entrepreneurship and inclusive growth ; highlighted priority sectors for American investors — renewable energy, agro-industry, technology, infrastructure — and major assets such as a young population, a vast reservoir of natural resources and ongoing regional integration ; cited Angola’s economic recovery, with 3.5% growth in the first quarter of 2025, as a reflection of the continent’s economic vitality ; welcomed the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), which he considers a strategic lever to stimulate investment flows and foster innovation.

a3849.speaker: Mekki ELMOGRABI, Sudanese press writer and media consultant
a3849.speech: Predicts that the implementation of the new U.S. conflict prevention strategy will be a "game-changer" and improve the image of the United States in the world, especially in Africa and third world countries, where the "image of the United States" as a maker of 'constructive chaos' - true or false - will be transformed into a new positive image."

a3849.speaker: Mekki ELMOGRABI, Sudanese press writer and media consultant
a3849.speech: In his article "5 Points and 5 Questions on the U.S. Strategy to Prevent Conflict and Promote Stability" published on the website of Global America and African Affairs, raised a question on how the U.S. would respond to the influence of China and Russia that contradicts this strategy, "the two countries always try to find their own shortcuts before the U.S. engages with third-world governments".

a3849.speaker: Mekki ELMOGRABI, Sudanese press writer and media consultant
a3849.speech: Comparing between push and pull factors of terrorism, asked how the strategy would address the adverse effects of neighboring and regional countries that the U.S. did not choose in the first phase: "the U.S. will act in one area within the strategy and possibly might begin a counterterrorism operation in a few miles distance while delivering tons of USAID assistance to the same tribe that spreads in another country," he argued ; Concluded that there are still some concerns, but this strategy has put U.S. foreign policy on the right track, and all of these issues will be addressed.

a4340.speaker: Government of Belgium
a4340.speech: Announced on Tuesday that Belgium will recognize Palestinian statehood and impose sanctions on Israel over its war in Gaza; the sanctions include a ban on imports of products from Jewish settlements in the West Bank and restrictions on consular assistance for Belgian nationals living in settlements considered illegal under international law.

a4340.speaker: Maxime Prevot, Belgian Foreign Minister (post on X)
a4340.speech: Wrote that in light of the "humanitarian tragedy in Gaza," Belgium has decided to "increase pressure on the Israeli government and Hamas terrorists." "This is not about punishing the Israeli people, but about ensuring that their government respects international and humanitarian law and takes action to change the situation on the ground." ; said Brussels will also review procurement involving Israeli companies and blacklist "two extremist Israeli ministers, several violent settlers, and Hamas leaders," and added that Belgium would push for the suspension of the EU's trade agreement with Israel.

a4340.speaker: Benjamin Netanyahu, Israeli Prime Minister
a4340.speech: Accused France and Australia last month of failing to tackle antisemitism, arguing that recognition of Palestine would only embolden Hamas.

a4340.speaker: Israel / West Jerusalem
a4340.speech: Has rejected UN warnings of famine in Gaza; West Jerusalem has pledged to allow the delivery of aid, but not through distribution points it claims are controlled by Hamas.

a4482.speaker: Cleo Diara, Cape Verdean actress
a4482.speech: On the Cape Verde she left and Portugal: "I always say that my image of Cape Verde, and one I don't want to be disturbed, is of playing during the holidays, of the neighbours, of my grandmother and my siblings, when most of the family was still together, because later, with emigration, some went to France, others to the United States, and we ended up separated. At 10 I came to Portugal, where I spend most of my life."

a4482.speaker: Cleo Diara, Cape Verdean actress
a4482.speech: On the in-between place that defines her as an artist: "I usually say that I have many waters. One of them is my mother, my sister, my friends. The other is Cape Verde, which for me is heart, water that moves inside me. The immigrant who always wants to feel that she belongs somewhere. Often we are here in Portugal, we are not seen as Portuguese and we want to have some land in which we can root our feet. Cape Verde is that place I want to reclaim."

a4482.speaker: Cleo Diara, Cape Verdean actress
a4482.speech: On resistance in her work: "I think black bodies in the diaspora have that experience, that resistance of being able to exist, to be who we are.
