Of telling stories in the first person, not always giving our body to other people's stories. Being able to speak of our own narrative without stereotypes, without the outside gaze." ; "For black people, it seems we are always starting something, and we are not. We are the continuation of something, of paths that have already been opened by other people. We have always existed, we have always contributed, we have always been part of it. Perhaps we were not written into history, perhaps there were certain erasures, but we always contributed, we always did."

a4482.speaker: Cleo Diara, Cape Verdean actress
a4482.speech: On the origins of the Aurora Negra project: "Isabel Zuaa, an actress who works here and in Brazil, contacted me and told me about a project she wanted to do. I mentioned Nadia Yracema and Ana Valentim and said it would be good for us to meet. At the time, we could not get funding to take the project forward, but that desire was planted there. Some time later, Nadia realised that applications had opened for the Amelia Rey Colaco Grant. We applied and we won. That is how Aurora Negra begins." ; "We do not see it that way [as a manifesto], but as a celebration. The celebration of our stories, of our experience, of our community, of our relationship with Portugal. Obviously, it has a bit of manifesto, of retelling history, when we invoke women who existed before, but above all, it is a celebration."

a4482.speaker: Cleo Diara, Cape Verdean actress
a4482.speech: On the film "O Riso e a Faca" and her Cannes Best Actress award: "It was an intense experience, because we filmed in Guinea-Bissau. It was three months, we were all displaced from our homes. Some moments were hard, but also very rewarding. It was the character to whom I gave the most of myself; I even lent my name." ; "I am understanding the award little by little, through other people's reactions, because everyone says it is big, 'you made history'. I gave, I gave a lot, I worked immensely, immensely so. I loved going to the film set, everything made sense. It was very rewarding and it took some time to understand everything that happened."

a4482.speaker: Cleo Diara, Cape Verdean actress
a4482.speech: On creating spaces for artists from Portuguese-speaking African countries: "It can be through a dream that I and the 'auroras' have, which is called Quilombo, a festival where we can bring together artists from Mozambique, Guinea, Angola, Cape Verde, and also from Brazil and Portugal. We have to keep working and opening space to talk more. A common space can be important for us to get to know one another again. We have many things in common that we do not need to speak about. I would very much like that space to exist. A space of experimentation, of new artists, together with established artists."

a4528.speaker: Prof. Dr. Kemalettin Aydın, Rector of the University of Health Sciences (UHS)
a4528.speech: In a powerful speech delivered online, emphasised that the occasion was more than a graduation, but a realisation of a civilisational ideal: “Today’s ceremony is not merely about awarding diplomas. It symbolises a bridge of civilisation built upon brotherhood and dedicated hearts. In regions neglected by the global system and drained by exploitative structures, we take pride in raising healthcare professionals equipped with knowledge, compassion, and a love for humanity” ; “As the UHS, we do more than educate—we forge bonds of the heart and fulfill a historical responsibility. Each healthcare worker trained in Somalia will also be a voice for the oppressed and a conscience for humanity” ; “On this meaningful occasion, I pay tribute to Sultan Abdulhamid II, who laid the intellectual foundations of our university centuries ago with the establishment of the Mekteb-i Tıbbiye-i Şahane, blending knowledge and compassion in a visionary mission” ; “I also express my deepest gratitude to President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who revived this vision in the modern era by founding our university in 2015 and leading the way in global health education” ; said the university will continue to serve as a “beacon of hope not only in Türkiye but in every corner of our shared cultural geography” and that it is a “service to God and humanity.”

a4528.speaker: Alper Aktaş, Türkiye’s Ambassador to Somalia
a4528.speech: Highlighted that relations between Türkiye and Somalia have grown beyond friendship into a strategic partnership; noted that the Mogadishu Recep Tayyip Erdoğan Faculty of Health Sciences has become a model institution for health education not only in Somalia but across the African continent; reaffirmed Türkiye’s commitment to continue supporting Somalia in the fields of health, education, and humanitarian aid.

a4528.speaker: Nura Mustaf Mukhtar, Somali Minister of Education
a4528.speech: Reflected on the deep-rooted partnership between the two countries, tracing it back to Türkiye’s humanitarian assistance to Somalia in 2011: “Today, we are witnessing how those seeds have grown into a strong tree”; expressed pride in the graduates—especially those from the Emergency Aid and Disaster Management Department—and congratulated all, with particular mention of those from the Nursing and Midwifery programmes.

a4528.speaker: Fowsiya Abdikadir, speaking on behalf of the graduates
a4528.speech: Stated that their education at UHS instilled not only academic knowledge but also a deep sense of responsibility: “We worked hard to reach this point. I am grateful to our university and everyone who supported us along the way.”

a4618.speaker: Local fire department (Myanmar), video release
a4618.speech: Released a video in which Naing Lin Tun, shirtless and covered in dust, appeared weak but conscious as he was fitted with an IV drip and taken away.

a4618.speaker: State-run MRTV
a4618.speech: Reported that the rescue in the city of Naypyitaw was carried out by a Turkish and local team and took more than nine hours.

a4618.speaker: State television MRTV
a4618.speech: Reported that 2,886 people have been reported dead in Myanmar and another 4,639 injured.

a4618.speaker: United Nations
a4618.speech: According to the UN, more than 3 million people were displaced from their homes and nearly 20 million in need even before the earthquake hit.

a4618.speaker: Three Brotherhood Alliance (militia group)
a4618.speech: Announced a unilateral one-month ceasefire on Tuesday to facilitate the humanitarian response.

a4618.speaker: National Unity Government (shadow opposition)
a4618.speech: Had already called a ceasefire for its forces.

a4618.speaker: Ta'ang National Liberation Army (opposition militia of the Brotherhood Alliance)
a4618.speech: Reported that the military fired on a relief convoy of nine Chinese Red Cross vehicles late Tuesday on a road in the northern part of Shan state near Ohn Ma Tee village, and said the Chinese Red Cross was bringing supplies to Mandalay and had reported its route to the military.

a4618.speaker: Maj. Gen. Zaw Min Tun, spokesman for the military regime
a4618.speech: Told state-run MRTV that the convoy had not notified authorities of its route ahead of time; while not mentioning the Red Cross, he said security forces had fired into the air to deter a convoy that refused to stop near Ohn Ma Tee village, the site of recent fighting with the TNLA.

a4618.speaker: Guo Jiakun, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson
a4618.speech: Did not comment on the attack, but said “relief supplies provided by the Red Cross Society of China to Myanmar have arrived in Myanmar and are on the way to Mandalay,” adding that “rescue personnel and supplies are safe.”

a4618.speaker: Tom Andrews, monitor on rights in Myanmar commissioned by the U.N.-backed Human Rights Council
a4618.speech: Said on X that military attacks must stop to facilitate aid: “The focus in Myanmar must be on saving lives, not taking them.”

a4618.speaker: Australia (government)
a4618.speech: Said on Wednesday it was providing another $4.5 million, in addition to $1.25 million it had already committed, and had a rapid response team on the ground.

a4618.speaker: Washington (U.S. government)
a4618.speech: Said on the weekend it would provide $2 million in emergency assistance.

a4618.speaker: Democratic Voice of Burma (independent outlet)
a4618.speech: Reported that in Singu township, about 65 kilometers north of Mandalay, 27 gold miners were killed in a cave-in.

a4618.speaker: Global New Light of Myanmar (government's official newspaper)
a4618.speech: Reported that in the area of Inle Lake, northeast of the capital, many people died when homes built on wooden stilts in the water collapsed in the earthquake, without providing specific figures.

a4757.speaker: Health officials and aid agencies
a4757.speech: Say more than 300,000 Somali children could miss lifesaving vaccines this year after the United States scaled back humanitarian funding.

a4757.speaker: Asha Abdullahi, nurse at a displacement camp on Mogadishu’s outskirts
a4757.speech: Said patient loads have doubled since January ; “We treat about 60 children a day. When vaccine stocks run dry, preventable diseases spread within weeks.”

a4757.speaker: Aid groups
a4757.speech: Warn the shortfall is pushing malnutrition rates beyond emergency thresholds.

a4757.speaker: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (latest bulletin)
a4757.speech: One in five children under five is acutely malnourished.

a4757.speaker: Farah Hassan, coordinator of relief efforts in Lower Shabelle
a4757.speech: Said dwindling resources have forced agencies to suspend mobile vaccination teams in remote districts ; “Families walk for hours to reach static clinics, only to find the fridges empty. Without immediate funds, we will see outbreaks and avoidable deaths.” ; “Somalis can survive drought if they receive basic support. What they cannot survive is losing that support when they need it most.”

a4757.speaker: The U.S. Agency for International Development
a4757.speech: Did not respond to requests for comment.

a4757.speaker: Humanitarian agencies
a4757.speech: Are appealing for an extra $1 billion this year to cover food, water and health needs across the Horn of Africa nation.

a5422.speaker: Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) 2024 Most Neglected Crises report
a5422.speech: Lists Cameroon, Mozambique and a host of other African nations as some of the most burdened by violence and displacement, but also the most invisible to donors; says millions of people who have been displaced and face food insecurity or lack shelter are receiving little aid because of “donor fatigue”, poor media coverage and little-to-no political resolution; of 34 countries analysed, the most “invisible” were Cameroon, Ethiopia, Mozambique, Burkina Faso, Mali, Uganda, Iran, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Honduras and Somalia; added that aside from funding, there was little progress on effective conflict resolution, disaster prevention and diplomatic engagement in all the affected countries; noted that aid funding dropped overall in 2024 ; “The shortfall between what was required to meet humanitarian needs in 2024 and what was delivered was a staggering $25 billion, meaning over half of all needs went unmet.”

a5422.speaker: Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) 2024 Most Neglected Crises report
a5422.speech: Noted that the aftershocks of the Tigray war merged with new intercommunal fighting in the Oromia and Amhara regions, creating a potent mix of crises which has seen 10 million people pushed out of their homes nationwide in Ethiopia ; reported that Cameroon’s displacement crisis was mentioned in fewer than 30,000 articles in English, Spanish, French and Arabic in 2024, compared with the Ukraine war, which was mentioned in 451,000 articles ; warned that shrinking aid could escalate friction between local communities and refugees in Uganda ; said Somalia received “dangerously low” funding in 2024.

a5422.speaker: Christelle Hure, NRC’s head of advocacy in West and Central Africa
a5422.speech: “Too many crises across the continent remain in the shadows – ignored because they don’t make headlines, or because they are not seen as of immediate strategic interest to international partners.” ; “Crises that knock on Europe’s door – as happened in 2015 [with mass immigration] – tend to receive the greatest media attention, while those far away remain not only out of sight but also out of mind.”

a5422.speaker: Beverly Ochieng, security analyst with UK-based intelligence firm Control Risks
a5422.speech: “The violence there is largely ignored because it’s not a direct threat to the central government,” adding that little has been done to negotiate peace in Cameroon: “There was a feeling initially that some of the secessionist leaders were trying to lobby Donald Trump to support their cause but they’ve just not received any attention.”

a5422.speaker: United Nations
a5422.speech: According to the UN, only 45 percent, or $168m of the $371m required, was raised to fund aid in Cameroon’s various crises.

a5422.speaker: Local media tallies (Mozambique)
a5422.speech: About 400 people died in the post-election violence in Mozambique, according to local media tallies.

a5422.speaker: Beverly Ochieng, security analyst with UK-based intelligence firm Control Risks
a5422.speech: Attributes shrinking aid to the three military-led countries of the West African Sahel, including Niger, partly to the hostile stances towards Western powers of the leaders there: “These military leaders are focused on economic development and they don’t even want to be seen as not being able to provide for their people … that makes it very difficult for any donors to approach them to provide help, or even for aid agencies to assess what the actual needs are.”

a5422.speaker: Christelle Hure (Hule) of the NRC
a5422.speech: Said the African Union (AU) must take the lead in resolving the continent’s multiple crises through political negotiations: “What is urgently needed today isn’t just more funding – it’s clear political commitment, not only from donors but crucially from the African Union and its member states.” ; added that countries also need to reduce administrative and regulatory barriers that hamper aid workers: “Easing these constraints, in close collaboration with authorities and the African Union, would greatly enhance the efficiency and impact of our collective response.”

a5423.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP)
a5423.speech: Says famine looms in Somalia without a funding boost; believes that about 1.26 million children under the age of five need immediate support, of which 466,000 will likely be severely acutely malnourished this year and at risk of death.

a5423.speaker: IPC (international food security classification system)
a5423.speech: According to the IPC, acute hunger is level three on a scale of one to five, with level five denoting famine and level four, severe acute malnutrition.

a5423.speaker: Jean-Martin Bauer, WFP spokesperson
a5423.speech: “We have learned in Somalia from past experience that that delays can be deadly, and we need resources to provide support to these very vulnerable groups,” speaking from Rome; called on donors and partners to increase funding to the country of 19 million people ; said just 12 per cent of the $1.4 billion overall appeal for Somalia has been funded so far ; stressed that a combination of in-kind food assistance and cash-based transfers is needed to mitigate the worst effects of the crisis: “When you are facing a crisis like the one we are worried about in Somalia, we need all types of resources to be put at play to avert the worst.”

a5423.speaker: Jean-Martin Bauer, WFP spokesperson
a5423.speech: Said two consecutive failed crop seasons last year resulted in harvests 45 per cent below-average yields.

a5423.speaker: Weather forecasters
a5423.speech: Predict another drought from April to June.

a5423.speaker: Humanitarians
a5423.speech: Warn that malnutrition is likely to worsen due to disease outbreaks and reduced food access.

a5456.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5456.speech: Is heard stating that Egypt may blow up the Dam ; is also heard urging Prime Minister Hamdok to intervene on behalf of Ethiopia, citing the recent aid cuts from the United States as a consequence of Ethiopia commencing with Dam filling.

a5456.speaker: Aaron Salzberg, Wilson Centre Global Fellow and director of the Water Institute at the University of North Carolina (UNC)
a5456.speech: Stated that the chances for the militarisation of the Nile are less likely than presumed by outside observers, as long as diplomatic discussions persist between the countries involved; continued negotiations between Ethiopia and Egypt indicate the low likelihood of the situation escalating into war.

a5456.speaker: Aaron Salzberg, Wilson Centre Global Fellow and director of the Water Institute at the University of North Carolina (UNC)
a5456.speech: Highlighted the institutionalisation of diplomacy between the two countries as a way forward, citing the example of the International Boundary & Water Commission, the formal body between the United States and Mexico on water diplomacy, as a means of dealing with evolving issues between two countries, which could also serve to improve regional coordination efforts so long as it maintains flexibility in rules and design ; said institutionalising the process could additionally help resolve tensions brought about by the hegemony of Egypt in the Nile basin, and suggested that the two countries, with the role of an invisible mediator in the background, could resolve their issues amicably.

a5456.speaker: Dina Mufti, spokesperson for the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a5456.speech: Said Ethiopia looks forward to commencing the negotiations, which have currently been paused: "We want the Nile River to be a source of cooperation and regional integration," adding that the country is open to any forums in the future. "But the equitable and rational use of the resource are two basic elements that require agreement before any other decisions."

a5456.speaker: Dina Mufti, spokesperson for the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a5456.speech: "We aren't a signatory to that agreement" [the 1959 Nile Waters Agreement]. "And Ethiopia is entitled to the use of resources considering that Abbay is the largest contributor to the Nile."

a5456.speaker: Dina Mufti, spokesperson for the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a5456.speech: "The Dam is equated with the sovereignty of the country. It is being built by Ethiopian people with their energy, money and technology."

a5456.speaker: Dina Mufti, spokesperson for the Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs
a5456.speech: "Africans can solve their own problems, and we believe that the African Union is doing so in a humble and honest method from which we require only the role of a facilitator."

a5456.speaker: Abiy Ahmed (PhD), Prime Minister of Ethiopia (statement)
a5456.speech: "Occasional statements of belligerent threats to have Ethiopia succumb to unfair terms still abound," reads the statement, which went on to say that the GERD has been an answer to a generation's quest for an equitable and reasonable utilisation of the Abbay and other rivers contributing to the Nile from Ethiopia.

a5456.speaker: Dejen Yemane, lecturer at Wollo University School of Law specialising in international law
a5456.speech: Believes that the three riparian countries have taken the wrong path over the negotiations of the Dam: "There has never been any kind of bilateral or trilateral negotiations in the history of a unilateral project on a transboundary water. A basin-wide legal framework agreement might be looked at for a sustainable and equitable use of the water." He referred to the 2010 Cooperative Framework Agreement (CFA), signed by five upstream countries, save Sudan and Egypt, as an ideal framework between the three countries.

a5456.speaker: Dejen Yemane, lecturer at Wollo University School of Law specialising in international law
a5456.speech: "The terms of negotiation forwarded from the Egyptians are intolerable for Ethiopia, and it breaches the country's sovereignty and future rights on the water. GERD is currently being used as the hostage." ; Said a firm stance by Ethiopia will give Egypt no options but to sign the CFA, and added that establishing a permanent institution is important in addressing the wants and needs of the riparian countries in the future.

a5471.speaker: South Sudan National Bureau of Standards (SSNBS) (Facebook post)
a5471.speech: Reiterated its call to all importers, partners, stakeholders, and the general public to adhere strictly to national quality and safety regulations ; stated that their mandate is to ensure that only safe, high-quality, and standard-compliant products enter the South Sudanese market ; expressed its strong commitment to preventing harmful or non-compliant products from entering South Sudan's markets by ensuring continuous inspections.

a5471.speaker: SSNBS officials (anonymous)
a5471.speech: According to officials, the goods were intercepted at the Nimule border point during routine inspections aimed at protecting consumers and ensuring product quality.

a5877.speaker: Meles Alem Tekea, Ethiopian Ambassador to Kenya
a5877.speech: Confirmed in a statement that his country will not stop its mission in Nairobi: "The Nairobi mission will not be closed. Ethiopia's neighbouring countries such as Kenya remains a priority to the Ethiopian foreign policy." ; Told the local media in Kenya that PM Abiy Ahmed had been misquoted during his address to Parliament last week.

a5877.speaker: Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopian Prime Minister
a5877.speech: In a briefing to Ethiopian lawmakers on Monday said Ethiopia will shut down several embassies to manage costs and have most diplomats work as non-resident ambassadors: "Ethiopia shouldn't have 60 or so embassies and consulates in the present moment. Instead of throwing US dollars everywhere ... at least 30 of the embassies should be closed ... the ambassadors should instead be here" ; "The Ethiopian ambassador in Kenya, for example, probably meets the Kenyan foreign minister once a year or once in two years." ; "With the current situation Ethiopia is in, the country doesn't need to have as many as 60 or so embassies and consulates."

a5877.speaker: Abiy Ahmed, Ethiopian Prime Minister
a5877.speech: Said that instead of hiring drivers, government ministers will be required to drive themselves: "What we want is a person who gets wet in the mud and runs while reforming the country."

a6148.speaker: Tommy Pigott, Deputy State Department spokesman
a6148.speech: "We're not going to be part of organizations that pursue policies that hamper the United States," Deputy State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott told reporters Thursday.

a6148.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary General
a6148.speech: He warned in January it was facing "a full-blown liquidity crisis."

a6148.speaker: Eugene Chen, senior fellow at New York University's Center on International Cooperation
a6148.speech: "UN 80 is in large part a reaction from the Secretary General to the kind of challenges posed by the second Trump administration," said Eugene Chen.

a6148.speaker: Brett Schaefer, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute
a6148.speech: "There are some things that the UN does that arguably should be increased in terms of resources. And then there are some things that the UN shouldn't be decreasing but eliminating altogether." He cited the UN's nuclear watchdog and the World Food Program as contributing significantly to US interests and singled out the Food and Agriculture Organization and Human Rights Council as having mandates at odds with American policy.

a6148.speaker: UN staff in Geneva
a6148.speech: Announced last week they passed a motion of no confidence in Guterres and the plan.

a6148.speaker: Ian Richards, president of the UN Staff Union in Geneva
a6148.speech: "Staff felt its slash and burn approach lacked focus, had no strategic purpose, and was making the UN more top-heavy and bloated," Ian Richards posted on LinkedIn about the UN 80 report.

a6148.speaker: Eugene Chen, senior fellow at New York University's Center on International Cooperation
a6148.speech: That vote has largely symbolic importance, according to NYU's Chen. Still, Guterres' efforts to get ahead of the inevitable cuts that reductions in US support will bring could help the UN adapt, he added. "Maybe that's a silver lining. We'll all be primed for reform."

a6149.speaker: Federal High Court, Port Harcourt (court record)
a6149.speech: Has fixed May 20, 2025, for the hearing of contempt proceedings filed against the Managing Directors of General Hydrocarbons and Century Energy Limited and others, over alleged disobedience to the orders of the court.

a6149.speaker: Justice A.T. Mohamed, Federal High Court (court order of December 18, 2024)
a6149.speech: Ordered the arrest and detention of 150,000 barrels of Crude oil which belongs to GHL on board an oil tanker, M.T. Tamara Tokoni, as security for the plaintiff's claim: "an order is hereby made directing the admiralty marshal with the assistance of the Nigerian Navy, and the Harbour Master of Nigerian Ports Authority to arrest and detain the Cargo of 150,000 barrels of Crude Oil herein sued as 1st defendant respondent and currently onboard MT. Tamara Tokoni IMO: NO 8302131 ... be arrested and remain under arrest pending further orders or further directions of this Honourable Court." ; "An Order is hereby made directing that the Cargo of 150,000 Barrels of Crude Oil ... be released from arrest only upon payment of all sums claimed in the writ of summons into Court or pending the provision of an acceptable Bank Guarantee, to the Deputy Chief Registrar of this Honourable Court, in the sum of: A total sum of USD$1,647,975 ... being unpaid Hire due to the plaintiff from the 2nd defendant for the Hire of the plaintiffs Ships: MV DONNY & MV OCEAN MERIT ... The sum of USD$60,000.00 ... Cost of redelivery of vessel ... The sum of USD$50,000 ... on the footing of General damages, to be issued by First Bank of Nigeria Plc, Zenith Bank Plc, United Bank for Africa Plc or any other First-Class Nigerian Bank acceptable to the Applicant."

a6149.speaker: Godpower Anuba, Plaintiff's Operations Supervisor (affidavit of facts and urgency)
a6149.speech: "that I know as a fact that, on the 18/12/2024, sequel to the originating processes filed in this suit together with a motion Exparte for the arrest and detention of the 1st defendant, this court directed the admiralty marshal with the assistance of the Nigeria Navy, and the Harbour Master of the Nigeria Ports authority to arrest and detain the 1st defendant pending the provision of an acceptable bank guarantee to secure plaintiff's claim as writ of summons"

a6209.speaker: Meri Rantanen, Finnish Interior Minister (statement)
a6209.speech: Affirms that Finland wishes to develop a functioning partnership with Somalia that serves both countries’ interests: “Finland’s top priority is to establish effective return arrangements and develop related cooperation with Somalia.” ; Elucidated that development cooperation is conditional on countries’ agreement to repatriate their citizens upon Finland’s request.

a6209.speaker: Government of Somalia (no official statement)
a6209.speech: Apart from a post on Somalia’s Office of the Prime Minister’s Facebook page, Somalia has not issued any official statement clarifying the Finnish Interior Minister’s official visit to Somalia so far and whether they discussed return arrangements.

a6209.speaker: Finnish Refugee Council
a6209.speech: Estimates the number of undocumented people in Finland at about 3,000-6,000 individuals.

a6209.speaker: Analysts (Finland, unnamed)
a6209.speech: Believe that this number is not a burden to the Finnish governmental and social system, but that the aim of bringing up the Somalia topic now is solely to advance the Finns Party’s campaign for the upcoming county and municipal elections in April 2025 ; Define Minister Rantanen’s motivation to visit Somalia as a way to promote her party in the coming county and municipal elections as an attempt to coax more voters.

a6209.speaker: Riikka Purra, Chairperson of the Finns Party and Finland’s Finance Minister (statement on X)
a6209.speech: Welcomed Minister Rantanen’s move to arrange a return mechanism for undocumented Somali nationals in Finland: “Minister of the Interior Rantanen visited Somalia. Promoting returns. Bilateral development cooperation in the Somalia Country Program is at a standstill because returns have not worked.”

a6209.speaker: Sebastian Tynkkynen, Member of the European Parliament and Finns Party member
a6209.speech: Praised Minister Rantanen’s attempt to seek a way to deport asylum seekers from Somalia: “Mari visited Somalia to promote the return of Somalis to their homeland. There is a woman who does.”

a6209.speaker: Ali Hassan, 35-year-old Somali refugee in Finland
a6209.speech: Shared his story of having his asylum application rejected almost half a dozen times during his 8-year stay in Finland, and said he believes good days are ahead: “Thanks to Allah, I got married here in Finland, have three children and a lovely wife. This gives me a reason to live and express my gratitude to Allah and my wife, who supports me in every circumstance.”

a6209.speaker: Article published by the Rift Valley Institute
a6209.speech: In 2018 Somali migrants around the world remitted 1.3 billion USD.

a6257.speaker: South32 (quarterly report)
a6257.speech: “Despite our efforts, negotiations have not progressed to provide confidence that Mozal Aluminium will secure sufficient and affordable electricity supply beyond March 2026” ; “Without the required electricity supply, we expect that Mozal Aluminium will be placed on care and maintenance at the end of the current agreement.”

a6257.speaker: South32 (Australian company that owns the plant)
a6257.speech: Said in the document that it is continuing to “actively engage” with Mozambique's government, with the Cahora Bassa Hydroelectric Plant (HCB) and with South Africa's Eskom – which buys electricity from HCB and sells it to Mozal – “on securing sufficient and affordable electricity for Mozal.”

a6257.speaker: South32 (quarterly report)
a6257.speech: States that Mozal's saleable production increased by 3% to 93,000 tonnes in the third quarter of 2025, compared to the previous quarter, “with the smelter operating near its maximum technical capacity,” prior to the decision in August “to stop pot relining due to the uncertainty of future electricity supply beyond March 2026”; the production projection for the 2026 fiscal year remains unchanged at 240,000 tonnes, “based on operations continuing to March 2026, when the current electricity supply agreement expires.”

a6257.speaker: Inocêncio Impissa, spokesperson for the Council of Ministers (Cabinet) of Mozambique
a6257.speech: “Mozambique's government continues and will naturally continue to, firstly, cherish Mozal and, secondly, it will continue to negotiate to improve the terms of negotiation and that it will continue to produce in Mozambique, with all the necessary facilities, but that there will be no harm to either party”; he added that Mozambique's government was informed of the risks associated with the crisis in Mozambique's largest industrial plant and of the cancellation of contracts by some of Mozal's suppliers, but clarified that the situation had nothing to do with the ongoing negotiations.

a6257.speaker: Mozal
a6257.speech: Announced in August that it intended to cut investment and lay off contracted contractors, keeping the operation going until March, claiming it was unable to continue.

a6257.speaker: Mozambique's Confederation of Economic Associations (CTA)
a6257.speech: Revealed that Mozal had “suddenly” cancelled contracts with around 20 companies, leaving at least one thousand workers unemployed.

a6257.speaker: Mozambique's government
a6257.speech: On 22 August, considered the tax contribution of its largest industry to be extremely low and expressed interest in proceeding with a review of its obligations in this area.

a6257.speaker: Daniel Chapo, Mozambican President
a6257.speech: On 18 August, said that the energy tariffs proposed by Mozal, Mozambique's largest industry, would lead to the collapse of HCB, in response to the threat of the aluminium smelting plant's closure in 2026.

a6257.speaker: Lusa (news agency report)
a6257.speech: Reported in February 2024 that Mozambique's government intends to repatriate the electricity it has been exporting from HCB to South Africa since 1979 for domestic use from 2030, as stated in the Strategy for Energy Transition in Mozambique until 2050.

a6299.speaker: Zahra Mohamed Ahmad ("Mama Zahra"), Somali human rights defender, founder of the Somali Women Development Center (SWDC)
a6299.speech: Said she has fought since returning to Somalia in 2000 for "justice, equality, and Somali unity" ; said her biggest loss came when her only son was killed by unknown men who stopped him as he was walking along one of the streets of Mogadishu ; "The gloomy ugly days that followed the ouster of the former Siad Barre regime, the days our children were dying for starvation and famine, the days mothers, children, and the old people dying on the streets fleeing from their homes, are still fresh in my memory" ; "And every year March 8 reminds many Somali women of the plight conditions they have gone through, in which many of them still live."

a6299.speaker: US State Department
a6299.speech: In 2021 recognized her exceptional bravery in defending the rights of the most vulnerable and awarded her the International Women of Courage Award.

a6299.speaker: Duniyo Mohamed Ali, Somali woman activist in Mogadishu
a6299.speech: "After the civil war broke out in 1991, the Somali women were the saviors of their families. They built schools and smaller clinics; mediated peace talks between clans; and became entrepreneurs to get bread on the tables of their families."

a6299.speaker: Kafi Ali Jire, chairperson of the Bari Region Women's Organization
a6299.speech: Said they could not celebrate the day with music and events because of the ongoing Puntland war with ISIS ; "Many women are mourning for the deaths of their husbands in the battle; others are sad because their husbands were injured, and many others whose husbands, sons and brothers are on the front lines are worrying about the safety of their loved ones, so instead of celebrating with colored events, [annual celebrations of the day that used to be held with arts, food and politicians], we have decided to dedicate the day to support our brave soldiers."

a6299.speaker: Lul Mohamed Sheikh, women's rights activist in Mogadishu
a6299.speech: "As of today, female candidates have secured only half the needed seats to reach the quota" ; "Our dream was that each community with three or more seats should have allocated one seat for the women. It sadly did not happen." ; Said the social and cultural norms that prevented women from getting constitutionally allocated seats are still in place ; "Clan elders, who play a key role in selecting potential lawmakers, have been blocking women from seeking office" ; "Other challenges include that the country's leaders do not nominate a good number of women into the top political offices and lack of unity among women."

a6299.speaker: Somali officials and the United Nations' humanitarian agencies
a6299.speech: Said this week that currently 3.4 million people are acutely food insecure, and this number is projected to rise to 4.4 million between April and June - nearly a quarter of the population.

a6299.speaker: World Food Program (WFP)
a6299.speech: Estimates that approximately 1.7 million children under the age of five require immediate support, with 466,000 likely to be severely acutely malnourished and at risk of death this year.

a6299.speaker: Jean-Martin Bauer, WFP spokesperson
a6299.speech: "We have learned in Somalia from past experience that delays can be deadly, and we need resources to provide support to these very vulnerable groups" ; He urged donors and partners to increase funding for the country of 19 million people as it faces this escalating crisis.

a6329.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP) and UNICEF
a6329.speech: Issued a warning on Thursday, reporting that at least 60,000 children in Upper Nile State, South Sudan, are at risk of death from malnutrition, a crisis aggravated by persistent fighting that prevents the delivery of humanitarian aid. ; WFP and UNICEF said in separate statements that Upper Nile currently has the highest malnutrition rates in the country, with more than 300,000 children affected by moderate or severe malnutrition over the past twelve months.

a6329.speaker: Mary-Ellen McGroarty, WFP representative in South Sudan
a6329.speech: “Children are always the first victims of crises. If we cannot deliver nutritional products, malnutrition risks worsening in areas already on the brink.” ; “Upper Nile is already one of the regions most affected by hunger. In these conditions, every day counts for a malnourished child who urgently needs treatment.”

a6359.speaker: Joyce Msuya, interim chief of the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
a6359.speech: Addressing the UNSC on Tuesday, Joyce Msuya described Israel’s monthlong ground offensive and ongoing siege of northern Gaza as an “intensified, extreme, and accelerated version of the horrors of the past year” in the Palestinian territory. Palestinian civilians have been driven from their homes by Israel’s military and “forced to witness their family members killed, burned and buried alive” in Gaza, which Msuya described as “a wasteland of rubble”. ; “We are witnessing acts reminiscent of the gravest international crimes,” she warned the council meeting. ; “The daily cruelty we see in Gaza seems to have no limits,” she said, firmly pointing the finger of blame at Israel for blocking aid from entering Gaza’s besieged north. ; “As I brief you, Israeli authorities are blocking humanitarian assistance from entering North Gaza, where fighting continues and around 75 000 people remain with dwindling water and food supplies,” she said. ; “What distinction was made and what precautions were taken, if more than 70 percent of civilian housing is either damaged or destroyed?”

a6359.speaker: International food security experts (report)
a6359.speech: a report by international food security experts on Friday who said the humanitarian situation in Gaza was “extremely grave and rapidly deteriorating” and warned of an imminent famine in parts of the north.

a6359.speaker: Danny Danon, Israel’s UN ambassador
a6359.speech: called the reports of possible famine in northern Gaza “baseless and slanderous”. He told reporters before the UNSC meeting that the situation in Gaza, including the north, has shown improvement since October.

a6359.speaker: Stephane Dujarric, UN spokesman
a6359.speech: said October saw the lowest amount of humanitarian aid enter Gaza this year, and the war-torn enclave had received “nowhere near what we need to support more than two million Palestinians”. Dujarric said that for a second month, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) was only able to reach half the people who rely on UN assistance in Gaza, and only with reduced rations.

a6359.speaker: Stephane Dujarric, UN spokesman
a6359.speech: The other trucks in the aid convoy were unable to make their deliveries because of delays in receiving authorisation from Israeli authorities as well as due to crowds of desperately hungry people waiting along the convoy’s route, Dujarric said. The delivery was the first time in more than a month that people in Beit Hanoon had received any food assistance, he said. ; The WFP had planned another mission to Beit Hanoon to reach the rest of the shelters and the hospital on Tuesday, but he said that “those missions have been denied” by Israel. ; “We continue to call for the immediate opening of more land routes into Gaza and for the lifting of administrative and physical restrictions within Gaza to efficiently reach the most vulnerable people and areas,” Dujarric said.

a6359.speaker: Riyad Mansour, Palestine’s UN envoy
a6359.speech: told the UNSC meeting that Israel has chosen to perpetrate “famine as a method of war” in a process of ethnic cleansing in Gaza. “Everything we warned against, everything Israel denied, is happening before our eyes,” he said. “We are at the last stages of an orchestrated plan to empty wide areas of Gaza from its Palestinian population.”

a6531.speaker: Rilwan Sorunke, Founder of the Policy Vault Project and Principal at Dev-Afrique Development Advisors
a6531.speech: Argues that Lagos's real sanitation crisis runs deeper than building more toilets, and that it is data-shaped: “Sanitation does not get the same attention or investment as roads, electricity, or even water” ; “It is treated like the stepchild of urban infrastructure.”

a6531.speaker: Rilwan Sorunke, Founder of the Policy Vault Project and Principal at Dev-Afrique Development Advisors
a6531.speech: His verdict on Lagos's sanitation situation is blunt — the city is flying blind: “Most sanitation systems in Lagos, pit latrines, septic tanks, container toilets, are not connected to sewers and are barely tracked. We don't know where they are, how often they are serviced, or where the waste ends up. That's a public health disaster waiting to happen.” ; “There is no integrated sanitation data platform. Decision-makers are working without the full picture.” ; warns “Without accurate, up-to-date data, interventions become guesswork. And in public health, guesswork kills.”

a6531.speaker: 2024 report released by Dev-Afrique
a6531.speech: Found that Lagos's sanitation data systems are woefully underdeveloped, and that the city's only baseline mapping exercise, conducted in 2022, was fragmented and too shallow to drive meaningful policy.

a6531.speaker: Rilwan Sorunke, Founder of the Policy Vault Project and Principal at Dev-Afrique Development Advisors
a6531.speech: Says Lagos lags behind peer African cities that have embraced data as the foundation for service delivery, citing Zambia's National Water Supply and Sanitation Council (NWASCO), which mandates utilities to map sanitation coverage and report on performance, and Kenya's digital platforms MajiData and WARIS, which track service levels in real time: “These countries treat data not as a luxury but as a necessity. Lagos must do the same.”

a6531.speaker: Rilwan Sorunke, Founder of the Policy Vault Project and Principal at Dev-Afrique Development Advisors
a6531.speech: Outlines three urgent steps for Lagos: build a citywide sanitation data hub, a central platform aggregating data from local governments, private waste operators, community health officers and NGOs, supporting real-time dashboards, GIS mapping and performance monitoring; deploy utility-ready data tools such as mWater, KoboCollect or ERP systems like EDAMS, already used in Uganda and Zambia, to help field workers gather geotagged data and track services at the household level; and institutionalise monitoring and evaluation, with dedicated M&E teams trained in data literacy and GIS embedded within agencies and empowered to act on insights.

a6531.speaker: Rilwan Sorunke, Founder of the Policy Vault Project and Principal at Dev-Afrique Development Advisors
a6531.speech: Is realistic about political and financial commitment, noting that with traditional donors like USAID pulling back from direct service funding, Lagos must rely on its own budget and political will: “This is not about luxury tech. It's about public health, governance, and equity. Lagos must train people, develop systems, and sustain them. Otherwise, the same communities will keep paying the price.” ; “Lives. Dignity. Wasted resources.” ; concludes “Lagos doesn't have a toilet problem. It has a data problem.”

a6631.speaker: U.S. State Department (annual Human Rights Practices report)
a6631.speech: Accused the United Kingdom of having “significant human rights issues,” including restrictions on free speech. The report claimed that human rights conditions in the UK “worsened” in 2024, citing “credible reports of serious restrictions on freedom of expression,” alongside “crimes, violence, or threats of violence motivated by antisemitism” following the October 7 Hamas attack against Israel. While the report acknowledged that free speech is “generally provided for” in Britain, it points to “specific areas of concern” involving limits on “political speech deemed ‘hateful’ or ‘offensive.’” The assessment singled out Britain’s public space protection orders and “safe access zones” around abortion clinics, and criticises the UK’s Online Safety Act, accusing ministers of intervening in ways that could “chill speech” about the 2024 Southport murders.

a6631.speaker: Sky News
a6631.speech: Cited as the source for the report's claims about human rights conditions in the UK worsening in 2024.

a6631.speaker: UK Home Office
a6631.speech: Says the public space protection orders and “safe access zones” measures are designed to protect women from harassment or distress.

a6631.speaker: UK ministers
a6631.speech: Defended the legislation as a child protection measure, with some suggesting that opponents are “on the side of predators.”

a6631.speaker: JD Vance, US Vice President
a6631.speech: Last week, during a meeting with Foreign Secretary David Lammy in Kent, warned he did not want the UK to go down a “very dark path” of losing free speech; echoing earlier criticisms he made during a February speech at the Munich Security Conference.

a6631.speaker: Keir Starmer, UK Prime Minister
a6631.speech: Has repeatedly defended the UK’s record, clashing with Mr Vance during a White House summit earlier this year: “We’ve had free speech for a very long time, it will last a long time, and we are very proud of that.”

a6631.speaker: UK government spokesperson
a6631.speech: In a response to the report, was quoted as saying, “Free speech is vital for democracy around the world, including here in the UK, and we are proud to uphold freedoms whilst keeping our citizens safe.”

a6631.speaker: Nigel Farage and Elon Musk
a6631.speech: The State Department’s conclusions mirror accusations made by Nigel Farage and tech billionaire Elon Musk.

a6638.speaker: Scott Perry, US Representative (Pennsylvania)
a6638.speech: Accused the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) of funding terrorist organisations. According to him, USAID spends 697 million dollars every year, not counting the remittances to support terrorist groups such as ISIS, ISIS-K and their training camps. These accusations were made during hearings of the Committee on Government Efficiency (DOGE), meetings held on 13 February.

a6906.speaker: The Wall Street Journal
a6906.speech: The Wall Street Journal analysed the enormous spending by the United States on aid to foreign states. And support for African countries turned out to be one of the least successful.

a7364.speaker: Transportes Aereos de Cabo Verde (TACV)
a7364.speech: Has just announced, with a visible effort at media promotion, a new "international tender" to hire consultants to draw up a strategy for repositioning the company between 2026 and 2031.

a7364.speaker: TACV (official communique on the tender)
a7364.speech: According to the official communique, the study will serve to reposition TACV in a more competitive post-COVID market.

a7364.speaker: TACV tender document / Terms of Reference
a7364.speech: Mentions the importance of TACV within the framework of the Strategic Plan for Sustainable Development (PEDS), in particular for the supposed "Sal hub", and states that the plan will "assess externalities" and "economic and social impact"; it requests consultants with an "innovative vision", does not address the question of solvency, is silent on any mechanism to make the execution of the future recommendations financially viable, and ignores the commitments made under the Single African Air Transport Market (SAATM), technological developments and ESG requirements.

a7364.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF), the GAO and the World Bank
a7364.speech: Have already warned that the company is not a vector of development but a contingent liability that distorts public finances.

a7507.speaker: Dom Ildo Fortes, Bishop of Mindelo
a7507.speech: "Cape Verde needs to slim down the machinery of the State, redefine priorities and invest in those who need it."

a7507.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a7507.speech: ordered the suspension of all of the country's international aid, with the exception of humanitarian food programmes and military aid to Israel and Egypt; the suspension is valid for a period of 90 days (from 25 January), giving the new Administration time to assess whether the programmes and aid are consistent with Trump's policies; under the "America First" agenda, only projects that demonstrably make the country safer and more prosperous may receive funding, and Trump intends to eliminate programmes related to initiatives promoting diversity, equity and inclusion, and also to reverse policies to combat climate change.

a7507.speaker: Ministry of Finance and Business Development (MFFE) data
a7507.speech: According to MFFE data, the State's current expenditure is expected to rise from about 41 billion ECV in 2015 to almost double that in 2025 (81.4 billion ECV), an increase of more than 98.5% ; also according to MFFE data, external debt is expected to rise from about 150 billion ECV in 2015 to about 208 billion ECV in 2025, an increase of about 39%.
